days.title: Infrastructure as Code: Declarative Model, Benefits and Providers Across Platforms

concepts.heading: What Infrastructure as Code Means
concepts.body: Infrastructure as code (IaC) means that networks, servers, databases and DNS records are described in text files that a tool turns into real resources, instead of being clicked together in a console by hand. Because the definition is a file, it can live in version control, be reviewed in a pull request, be run again tomorrow and be deleted when it is no longer needed. Terraform is HashiCorp's IaC tool: you write configuration in HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language, or JSON), and Terraform calls cloud and service APIs to make reality match it. A team that replaces a console runbook (open the VPC page, click Create, copy the ID into the next form) with a few `.tf` files has adopted IaC. One boundary matters: Terraform provisions infrastructure, it is not a configuration manager. Installing packages and editing config files inside a running server is the job of a separate configuration management tool or a prebuilt image; Terraform creates the server, and its docs describe an immutable approach where you change the definition and let the tool update or replace the object rather than patching it by hand.

concepts.heading: Declarative Versus Imperative
concepts.body: An imperative approach is a script of steps: create this subnet, then launch that VM, then attach the disk. Run it twice and you must handle the second run yourself, usually with checks like "if it exists, skip". A declarative approach describes the end state, and the tool works out the steps. Terraform is declarative: `resource "aws_s3_bucket" "logs" { bucket = "acme-audit-logs" }` says a bucket with that name should exist, nothing more. The first apply creates it; a second apply with no edits finds that reality already matches and does nothing ("No changes"). If you rename the bucket in the file, Terraform computes the difference and decides whether to update or replace it. Order is also inferred rather than written. When `aws_subnet.app` uses `aws_vpc.main.id`, Terraform builds a dependency graph from that reference and creates the VPC first, even if the subnet appears earlier in the file. Position in a file or across files never decides order; references (and `depends_on`, covered later) do.

concepts.heading: Benefits of IaC
concepts.body: The exam asks you to recognise the benefits and match them to a situation. Repeatability and consistency: the same definition builds identical dev, test and production networks, so subtle differences disappear, and short-lived environments become cheap (apply, run three days of QA, destroy). Version control: every change to a firewall rule is a commit with an author and a reason, which answers "who changed it and why" and lets you revert. Review before change: the plan shows exactly what will be created, changed or destroyed, so a reviewer can catch an unexpected destroy before it happens. Drift correction: if someone adds a port rule in the console, the next plan refreshes real objects and proposes changes that undo it, because the code is the source of truth. Reuse and self-service: a central team packages a standard as a module and many teams use it,. Terraform is not magic about cost or speed; the benefits come from the workflow.

concepts.heading: Write, Plan, Apply and State
concepts.body: HashiCorp describes the core workflow as three repeating steps. Write: author the configuration, normally in version control. Plan: Terraform compares the configuration with the state and the real objects and previews the changes without making any. Apply: Terraform carries them out in dependency order and records the result in state. State is a file (by default `terraform.tfstate`) that maps each resource block in your configuration to the real object it manages, and it is what lets Terraform compute only the changes needed instead of recreating everything. Other commands support this loop: `terraform init` prepares a directory, `validate` and `fmt` check and tidy code, and `destroy` ends the life of the infrastructure; they are not extra stages of the three-step description. For teams, HCP Terraform runs the same workflow in a consistent remote environment with shared state, secret handling and role-based access control, so nobody depends on one laptop.

concepts.heading: Providers, Multi-Cloud, Hybrid and Service-Agnostic
concepts.body: Terraform itself knows nothing about any cloud. Providers are plugins that translate resource blocks into API calls for one platform, and they are downloaded from the Terraform Registry (or a private source). That is why Terraform is called service-agnostic rather than only cloud-agnostic: any API-backed service with a provider, such as AWS, Azure, Kubernetes, vSphere, Datadog, GitHub or a DNS vendor, can be managed with the same language and the same write, plan, apply loop. One configuration can declare `provider "aws"` and `provider "google"` together; the prefix of each resource type (`aws_`, `google_`) selects its provider. Important limit: Terraform standardises the workflow, not the resource definitions. Changing only the provider block does not turn `aws_instance` into an Azure VM; you rewrite the resources for the new platform. References also work across providers: a DNS record at one vendor can use the address of a load balancer built on another cloud, and Terraform orders the two correctly. This is how hybrid estates (on-premises vSphere plus a public cloud) share one workflow.

examPoints: A question that says a team wants to "standardize the workflow" across clouds is testing that Terraform shares the process through providers, while resource types such as aws_instance and azurerm_linux_virtual_machine stay provider-specific.
A question where applying an unchanged configuration twice produces no changes is testing the declarative model: Terraform compares the desired end state with reality and acts only on the difference.
A question about installing software inside a running server or editing its config files points away from Terraform, which provisions infrastructure and is not a configuration manager.

quiz.q: A team writes aws_route53_record in one configuration whose value is the DNS name of a load balancer created by google_compute_forwarding_rule in the same configuration, using two provider blocks. What does Terraform do on apply?
choices: It rejects the configuration, because a reference may only connect resources that are handled by the same provider block in the file
It creates the DNS record first, because records for external vendors are always provisioned before the compute resources they point to
It creates the forwarding rule first, because the reference creates a dependency even across two different providers
It creates both in the order the blocks appear in the file, because Terraform follows file position when providers differ
quiz.explain: References build the dependency graph regardless of provider, so the forwarding rule is created first and its address feeds the record. Choice A is tempting because providers are separate plugins, but cross-provider references are exactly how multi-cloud estates are wired together.

quiz.q: An engineer describes a script that runs `create-subnet`, `launch-vm` and `attach-disk` in that fixed order and needs extra checks to be safe to run twice. Which statement classifies this and contrasts it with Terraform?
choices: It is declarative provisioning because the commands are in a fixed order; Terraform is imperative because it needs an explicit plan step
It is imperative provisioning where the author supplies the steps; Terraform is declarative and derives the steps from the desired end state
It is imperative provisioning, and Terraform is also imperative because each resource block is executed top to bottom in the file
It is configuration management because it touches several services; Terraform differs only by storing its steps in version control
quiz.explain: A step-by-step script is imperative; Terraform takes the desired end state and works out the steps and their order from references. Choice C is tempting because HCL looks like a list of commands, but the order of blocks has no effect.

days.recap: IaC puts infrastructure in versioned text; Terraform is declarative, orders work from references, and runs write, plan, apply with state mapping code to real objects. Providers make it service-agnostic, but resource types stay provider-specific and Terraform is not a configuration manager.

days.title: Providers: required_providers, Version Constraints, the Lock File and Aliases

concepts.heading: required_providers and Source Addresses
concepts.body: Terraform needs to know which plugins to install, and the `required_providers` block inside `terraform {}` says so. Each entry has a local name and a `source`: `aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws", version = "~> 5.2" }`. A source address is `[HOSTNAME/]NAMESPACE/TYPE`, and the short form `hashicorp/aws` means `registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws`. If you omit `source`, Terraform assumes the namespace `hashicorp` and the local name as the type, so a Datadog entry with only `version` makes init look for `hashicorp/datadog` and fail; third-party and partner providers always need an explicit source such as `DataDog/datadog`. The local name is what resource types use (`aws_instance` belongs to local name `aws`), and it only has to be unique inside that module, which allows two providers with similar names under different local names. The one exception is `terraform_remote_state`, which comes from the built-in `terraform` provider: never declare `hashicorp/terraform` in required_providers. In-house providers use the same shape, HOSTNAME/NAMESPACE/TYPE, even if installed from a filesystem mirror.

concepts.heading: Version Constraints
concepts.body: The `version` argument limits which provider releases Terraform may install. Operators: `=` (or no operator) exact, `!=` exclude, `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=` comparisons, and `~>` the pessimistic operator, which allows only the right-most number to grow. `~> 5.2` means at least 5.2 and below 6.0 (minor may grow); `~> 5.2.0` means at least 5.2.0 and below 5.3.0 (only patch). Several conditions separated by commas are ANDed, so `>= 3.0.0, < 3.5.0, != 3.4.2` accepts 3.4.9 but not 3.4.2 or 3.5.0. With no lock file, init picks the newest version that satisfies every condition. Example: with 5.1.0, 5.2.9, 5.40.1 and 6.0.0 available, `~> 5.2` selects 5.40.1. Pre-release versions such as `4.0.0-beta2` are ignored by range operators; to use one, pin that exact version. HashiCorp's guidance: a reusable module declares only a minimum (`>= 5.0`) so it fits many callers, and the root module sets the tighter `~>` range that actually decides what is installed.

concepts.heading: The Dependency Lock File
concepts.body: The first `terraform init` that selects provider versions writes `.terraform.lock.hcl` in the working directory. It records the exact version chosen and cryptographic hashes of the provider packages, so later runs by other people and CI install the same build instead of whatever is newest. Commit it to version control (do not commit the `.terraform` directory). Later inits obey the lock even if a newer release satisfies the constraint; `terraform init -upgrade` is how you deliberately move to the newest allowed version and rewrite the lock. If you change the constraint so the locked version no longer fits, init tells you to upgrade. A checksum mismatch error means the downloaded package differs from what was trusted at first use: investigate before updating the file. Installing from a network mirror records only the hashes for the local platform, so a Linux CI runner may fail on a lock created on macOS; run `terraform providers lock -platform=linux_amd64 -platform=darwin_arm64` to add the others. The lock file covers providers only, not modules; pin modules with an exact `version`. HCP Terraform honours the file too.

concepts.heading: Provider Configuration and Credentials
concepts.body: A `provider "aws" { region = "us-east-1" }` block configures a provider that has been required: region, endpoints, credentials and similar. Arguments may use variables and literals, but not values known only after apply (such as an attribute of a resource that does not exist yet), because Terraform must configure the provider before planning. Never hard-code access keys in the block, since the file is committed; use the provider's documented external sources such as environment variables (`AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`), shared credential files or an identity assumed by the runner, and mark any variable that does carry a secret as sensitive. Some providers need no provider block, because a default empty configuration is created for them, but most cloud providers need at least a region or project. Provider blocks belong in the root module: child modules inherit the parent's default configuration, and a shared module that contains its own `provider` block with a fixed region cannot be reused cleanly or removed with its module call.

concepts.heading: Aliases and Multiple Provider Configurations
concepts.body: To use the same provider more than once, for example two regions, give a second `provider "aws"` block `alias = "west"` and `region = "us-west-2"`. The block without an alias is the default configuration. A resource picks an aliased one with the unquoted meta-argument `provider = aws.west`; resources with no `provider` argument use the default. If every aws block has an alias there is no default, and a resource without `provider` gets an empty default configuration that usually fails. Modules do not see aliases automatically. To give a child module the west configuration, the caller passes `providers = { aws = aws.west }` (child name on the left, parent configuration on the right); if the module needs both a default and a second configuration, it declares `configuration_aliases = [aws.west]` inside its own `required_providers`. A common pattern is calling the same module twice with different providers maps to deploy it in two regions. Two different providers that share a type name (`hashicorp/http` and `mycorp/http`) need different local names, selected with `provider =`.

examPoints: A question where init fails to find hashicorp/<name> for a third-party provider is testing that a missing source defaults to the hashicorp namespace, so non-HashiCorp providers need an explicit source address.

A question that asks for the version installed under a constraint like ~> 5.2 or a comma-separated range is testing the rules: ~> lets only the last given number grow, commas are ANDed, and with no lock file the newest match wins.

A question about CI using different provider builds than developers, or about a platform hash error, points to committing .terraform.lock.hcl and to terraform providers lock -platform for other operating systems.

quiz.q: A root module requires `google = { source = "hashicorp/google", version = "~> 5.10.0" }`. No lock file exists, and the registry offers 5.9.4, 5.10.2, 5.10.7, 5.11.0 and 6.0.0. Which version does terraform init install?
choices: 5.11.0, because ~> allows the minor number to grow whenever the constraint begins with a major version of 5
6.0.0, because with no lock file Terraform ignores the constraint and installs the latest release available
5.10.2, because the first release that satisfies the constraint is chosen so that later patches are never applied
5.10.7, because ~> with three parts lets only the patch number grow and the newest matching release is chosen
quiz.explain: The three-part form allows only the patch to change, so 5.10.x is the range and the newest of those is 5.10.7. Choice A is tempting because `~> 5.10` (two parts) would allow 5.11.0, but adding the .0 locks the minor version.

quiz.q: A module block has `source = "./modules/queue"` and must create one queue in the default region and another in us-west-2. The root defines `provider "aws" {}` and `provider "aws" { alias = "west" }`. Which approach supports this?
choices: Call the module twice and pass `providers = { aws = aws.west }` in the second call so its resources use the aliased configuration
Add `provider = aws.west` as an argument to the second module block, because module calls accept the same meta-argument as resources
Declare a second provider block with the same alias inside the module, which then overrides the root module's configuration automatically
Set `alias = "west"` inside the module's required_providers entry, which makes Terraform create the queue in whichever region is cheaper
quiz.explain: Module calls use the `providers` map, with the child's name on the left and the parent's configuration on the right. Choice B is tempting because resources use `provider = ...`, but that argument is not valid on a module block.

days.recap: required_providers names plugins and sources (default namespace hashicorp); ~> grows only the last number, commas are ANDed, and the committed .terraform.lock.hcl pins versions and hashes until init -upgrade. Aliases: provider = aws.west for resources, providers = {...} for modules.

days.title: Terraform State: Why It Exists, What It Holds and How to Treat It

concepts.heading: Why Terraform Needs State
concepts.body: Configuration says what you want; the cloud holds what exists; Terraform needs a record that ties the two together. That record is state. First, state maps every resource instance in the configuration (for example `aws_instance.web`) to the real object (instance `i-0abc123`). Without that binding, Terraform cannot tell which of the existing objects belongs to which block, so a plan against an empty state proposes to create everything again, even if 40 resources already exist. Second, state stores metadata, most importantly dependency information. If you delete both `aws_subnet.app` and the instance that uses it from the configuration, there is nothing left in the code to say the instance must go first; the dependencies recorded in state let Terraform destroy in the right order. Third, state is a performance cache of resource attributes, which lets plans on large configurations avoid querying every object, and lets you skip refresh with `-refresh=false` at the risk of missing outside changes. Each of these cannot be derived from the configuration alone.

concepts.heading: What State Contains
concepts.body: By default Terraform writes state to `terraform.tfstate` in the working directory, in JSON; you should treat it as owned by Terraform and not edit it by hand. It holds, for each managed resource, its type, name, provider, the object's ID and all of its attributes as last known, plus the dependencies between resources, output values, and the Terraform and state-format version. It also stores a `serial` number and a lineage, which Terraform uses to detect when it would overwrite a newer copy with an older one. Data source results are recorded too. Because the whole attribute set is saved, state typically includes values you never wrote in your files, such as the generated ARN, the private IP or an auto-generated password. You can read it with `terraform show` (human-readable) or `terraform state list`, `terraform state show ADDRESS`; reading is fine, but editing the JSON directly can corrupt the mapping. The next days cover the commands that change state safely, such as `moved` blocks, `import` and `terraform state rm`.

concepts.heading: State and Secrets
concepts.body: State stores resource attributes in plain text, including those a provider marks sensitive. A database password you pass in, a generated private key, or an access token returned by an API all end up in the file, readable by anyone who can read it. Marking a variable or output `sensitive = true` hides the value in plan and apply output and in `terraform output`, but it does not remove it from state. Consequences: never commit `terraform.tfstate` to Git; store it where access is controlled and encrypted, which is one reason teams use a remote backend (an encrypted bucket with restricted access, or HCP Terraform, which also encrypts state and applies role-based access); and restrict who can read it as carefully as you restrict the secrets themselves. Saved plan files can also contain sensitive values for the same reason. Newer language features (ephemeral values and write-only arguments, Domain 4) are designed so that some secrets never reach state or plan files at all.

concepts.heading: Configuration, State and Real Infrastructure
concepts.body: Three things must be kept apart. The configuration is the desired state you write. The state is Terraform's last recorded view. The real infrastructure is what exists now. A plan first refreshes: it reads the current attributes of every object in state from the provider, updates Terraform's view in memory (state itself is only written on apply, or by `apply -refresh-only`), and then compares configuration against that refreshed view. So a manual console change is found at plan time, shown as drift, and by default reversed to match the code. A resource in the configuration with no state entry is planned for creation; an entry in state with no block is planned for destruction; an object created by hand and never imported is invisible to Terraform and untouched by plan or destroy. Keep a strict one-to-one binding: two resource blocks bound to the same remote object (the same instance ID) cause conflicting updates and a likely mess on the next apply or destroy.

concepts.heading: Losing, Sharing and Protecting State
concepts.body: If the only copy of state is lost, Terraform has no bindings: it will plan to create everything again, and the apply either duplicates resources or fails on name conflicts. Rebuilding means importing every object back, which is slow, so state needs backup and durable storage. When several people work together, a laptop copy is wrong: runs would plan from different views. Teams therefore keep state in a shared remote location with locking, covered in Domain 6, and the practical rules are those from this day: one state per set of resources, never in Git, access limited, and the file never edited by hand. Small configurations can run without remote state, and the default local state is fine for learning. In HCP Terraform, each workspace has its own state, with versions kept so earlier ones can be inspected or restored. When asked what Terraform stores that the code cannot provide, answer: the mapping from block to real object, resource metadata such as dependencies, and a cache of attributes.

examPoints: A question about why a plan wants to create 40 resources that already exist, after a state file was lost, is testing that state is the binding between configuration blocks and real objects.
A question where sensitive = true is offered as a way to keep a password out of the state file is testing that it only hides output in the CLI; state still stores the value in plain text.

A question that asks which TWO things state provides beyond the configuration points to the mapping of resources to remote objects and the metadata and cache (dependencies, attributes), not the desired state or the provider code.

quiz.q: A team commits terraform.tfstate to a private Git repository and marks the database password variable sensitive = true. A security reviewer objects. Which statement is accurate?
choices: The password is hashed inside the state file, so the repository is safe as long as the sensitive flag stays on every variable
The password is stored in plain text in the state file, so anyone with repository access can read it despite the sensitive flag
The password is absent from state because Terraform removes sensitive values before writing, so the objection is mistaken
The password is encrypted with the provider's key in the state file, and only a terraform apply run can decrypt it
quiz.explain: Sensitive only affects what the CLI prints; the value is written to state in plain text, so state needs controlled, encrypted storage and must not be committed. Choice C is tempting because the flag hides the value in plan output, but hiding is not removal.

quiz.q: A colleague deletes both aws_subnet.app and aws_instance.web (which uses the subnet) from the configuration and applies. The subnet cannot be removed until the instance is gone. How does Terraform know the order?
choices: It queries the provider API for the instance's subnet association, because state holds only names and never relationships
It destroys objects in alphabetical order of their addresses, retrying the failed ones until the cloud accepts the deletion
It reads the dependency information recorded in state, because the deleted blocks no longer exist in the configuration
It asks for confirmation of the order during apply, because a destroy without configuration cannot be ordered automatically
quiz.explain: State records dependencies, so deletions are ordered correctly even when the code that expressed them is gone. Choice A is tempting because refresh does call the API, but the ordering metadata comes from state.

days.recap: State maps each resource block to a real object, stores dependencies and an attribute cache, and holds secrets in plain text, so keep it out of Git and in controlled storage. Plan refreshes real infrastructure, compares it with the configuration, and lost state means everything looks new.

days.title: The Core Workflow and terraform init

concepts.heading: Write, Plan, Apply, Destroy in Practice
concepts.body: A typical session starts in a working directory with one or more `.tf` files. You run `terraform init` once (and again when providers, modules or the backend change), then loop: edit files, `terraform plan` to preview, `terraform apply` to execute, repeat. `terraform destroy` removes everything the state tracks when the environment is no longer needed. Plan reads the current state of existing remote objects, compares the configuration with the prior state, and proposes actions; it never changes infrastructure. Apply asks for a `yes` unless you pass a saved plan or `-auto-approve`. A plain `terraform plan` is only a preview: a later `terraform apply` builds a fresh plan, which may differ if something changed in between, so use `-out` when you must apply exactly what was reviewed (next day). If an apply fails halfway, for example a quota error on the database after the network and subnet were created, the successful pieces stay in state; fix the cause and apply again, and Terraform continues with what remains. Nothing is rolled back.

concepts.heading: What terraform init Does
concepts.body: `terraform init` prepares a working directory and is the first command to run after writing or cloning a configuration. It does three things: it initializes the backend (where state is stored, local by default), installs the providers listed in `required_providers` into `.terraform/providers` and records them in `.terraform.lock.hcl`, and downloads the modules referenced by `module` blocks into `.terraform/modules`. It never creates, changes or destroys infrastructure, and it is safe to run repeatedly; it will not delete your state. Init needs network access to the registry, unless a mirror is configured, and to the backend. A fresh clone must be initialised before `validate`, `plan` or `apply` will work; errors saying providers or modules are "not installed" mean init has not run in that directory. The `.terraform` directory is local, rebuilt by init and should not be committed, while `.terraform.lock.hcl` should be.

concepts.heading: -upgrade: Moving Past the Lock File
concepts.body: Plain `terraform init` is conservative. If the lock file pins a provider at 5.40.0 and your constraint is `~> 5.0`, init keeps installing 5.40.0 even after 5.41.0 is released, and a registry module with `version = "~> 3.0"` stays at the installed 3.1 when 3.2 appears. To pick up newer versions within your constraints, run `terraform init -upgrade`. It re-selects the newest provider versions that satisfy the constraints, rewrites the lock file with the new selection and hashes, and also updates installed modules from the registry (and re-fetches modules from VCS sources with moving references such as a branch). The flag cannot go beyond the constraints: if the constraint is `~> 5.0`, 6.0 will never be selected. Use it deliberately, as a reviewed change, commit the updated lock file, and run a plan afterwards to see what the new versions do. Do not use it merely to fix an installation problem; re-running plain init is enough for that.

concepts.heading: Backends and -migrate-state versus -reconfigure
concepts.body: A `backend` block inside `terraform {}` tells Terraform where state lives, for example `backend "s3"` with arguments such as `bucket` and `key`. Changing the backend block requires re-running init, and Terraform reports "backend configuration has changed" until you do. You then choose. `terraform init -migrate-state` copies the existing state from the old backend to the new one, the right choice when you add an s3 block to a project that has used local state and want to keep its state. `terraform init -reconfigure` tells Terraform to use the new settings without copying anything and to ignore the saved previous configuration; use it when the new location is intentionally empty or when you just edited a setting and do not want the old state moved. Mixing these up is a classic mistake: migrate when state must follow you, reconfigure when it must not. Both change where state is read from, so they should be run with the team's agreement. Backends are covered in depth on Day 13.

concepts.heading: -backend=false, -input=false and Other Init Options
concepts.body: `terraform init -backend=false` skips backend initialization but still installs providers and modules. It suits a CI job that must check a module before any credentials exist: run `init -backend=false`, then `terraform validate`, and no attempt is made to reach the state bucket. It is not suitable before a plan or apply because those need the backend. `-input=false` disables prompts, which pipelines use so a missing value fails fast instead of waiting forever. `-backend-config=...` supplies partial backend settings (file or key=value) so secrets and environment-specific values stay out of the committed block. `-lockfile=readonly` refuses to change the lock file, and `-get=false` skips module downloads. For the exam, remember the roles: plain init prepares, -upgrade moves versions forward within constraints, -migrate-state copies state, -reconfigure discards the old backend settings without copying, and -backend=false skips the backend.

examPoints: A question about newer provider versions not being installed although the constraint allows them is testing that the lock file keeps the selection until terraform init -upgrade is run.

A question where a backend block changes and the old state must or must not follow tests the pair: -migrate-state copies existing state to the new backend, -reconfigure adopts the new settings without copying.
A question about running validate in a pipeline before credentials exist points to terraform init -backend=false, which installs providers and modules but never contacts the backend.

quiz.q: A project has used local state for a year. An engineer adds a backend "s3" block and wants the existing state in the bucket without losing any resource tracking. Which action is correct?
choices: Run terraform init -reconfigure, which uploads the current state file to the new backend as part of switching
Run terraform init -upgrade, which moves state to the newest backend version available for the project
Run terraform init -migrate-state and confirm the copy of the existing state to the new backend when prompted
Run terraform plan, which detects the new backend and copies the state to it before the comparison
quiz.explain: -migrate-state is the option that copies existing state to the new backend. Choice A is tempting because reconfigure also switches the backend, but it deliberately does not copy state, so Terraform would see an empty one.

quiz.q: The lock file pins hashicorp/random at 3.5.1; the configuration says `version = "~> 3.5"`. Release 3.6.2 now exists. A new teammate clones the repository and runs terraform init. Which version do they get, and why?
choices: 3.6.2, because a new clone has no .terraform directory and therefore selects the newest release allowed
3.5.0, because the lowest version that matches the constraint is chosen whenever init runs on a clean clone
The command fails, because a locked version cannot be installed unless -upgrade confirms that it is still the newest
3.5.1, because init follows the committed lock file even though a newer release satisfies the constraint
quiz.explain: Init installs the version recorded in .terraform.lock.hcl; only -upgrade moves forward. Choice A is tempting because a clean clone looks like a first run, but the lock file travels with the repository and decides the version.

days.recap: The loop is write, plan, apply (destroy at the end). Init prepares the backend, providers and modules and never touches infrastructure; -upgrade moves versions within constraints, -migrate-state copies state, -reconfigure does not, and -backend=false skips the backend for credential-free checks.

days.title: validate, plan and apply: Saved Plans, Modes, Targets and Exit Codes

concepts.heading: terraform validate
concepts.body: `terraform validate` checks that the configuration is internally consistent: valid HCL syntax, known block and argument names, correct value types, and references to things that exist in the configuration, such as a variable or resource that is actually declared. It does not contact providers' remote APIs or any remote service, needs no credentials, and does not read state, which makes it a fast pre-commit or CI check. For the same reason it cannot tell whether an AMI ID exists, whether a bucket name is taken, or whether your credentials allow the action; those fail later, in plan or apply. Validate requires an initialized directory, because it needs the provider schemas; on a fresh clone run `terraform init` (or `init -backend=false`) first, otherwise it stops complaining that providers or modules are not installed, and the code is not at fault. Use `-json` for machine-readable results. Remember the split: syntax, types and references are caught by validate; remote facts surface at plan or apply.

concepts.heading: terraform plan
concepts.body: Plan creates an execution plan without changing anything: it refreshes the state of existing objects, compares the configuration with that view, and lists actions. Symbols: `+` create, `-` destroy, `~` update in place, `-/+` replace (destroy and create; "forces replacement" names the attribute). It prints a summary like "Plan: 1 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy." Three planning modes exist and only one can be chosen per run: the normal mode, `-destroy` (propose destroying everything), and `-refresh-only` (only update state to match reality, proposing no infrastructure changes). `-refresh=false` skips the refresh for speed on large configurations at the price of missing outside changes. `-target=ADDR` limits the plan to one resource and what it depends on; it is an exception tool for emergencies, not a workflow, and Terraform warns that the result may be incomplete. For automation, `-detailed-exitcode` makes the exit status 0 for an empty plan, 1 for an error and 2 when changes are present, so a scheduled drift check can fail only when something would change.

concepts.heading: Saved Plans with -out
concepts.body: A plain plan is a preview. If a pipeline must apply exactly what reviewers approved in a pull request, write the plan to a file: `terraform plan -out=tfplan`, review it, then `terraform apply tfplan`. The file records the changes and the variable values used, so apply does not re-plan and the result cannot drift from what was reviewed; if the state changed in between, apply refuses the stale plan. Inspect a saved plan without applying it using `terraform show tfplan` (add `-json` for tooling). Planning options such as `-target`, `-var` or `-refresh=false` belong on the plan command that creates the file; passing them to `apply tfplan` is rejected because the plan is already decided. Treat plan files like state: they may contain sensitive values, so store them securely and do not leave them in a public artifact bucket. A saved destroy plan works the same way: `terraform plan -destroy -out=destroy.tfplan`.

concepts.heading: terraform apply and Automation
concepts.body: Without arguments `terraform apply` creates a new plan, shows it and waits for you to type `yes`. With a saved plan file it applies that plan, and by default it does not ask again, because the review already happened. `-auto-approve` skips the prompt for a plan created in the same command, so use it only where nobody needs to look: ephemeral test environments or pipelines with a separate approval gate. Terraform ignores `-auto-approve` when you pass a saved plan file, because passing the file already counts as approval, so the plan must be reviewed first. In CI, `-input=false` prevents interactive prompts; if the job fails because Terraform cannot ask for confirmation, the fix is `-auto-approve` or a saved plan file. Apply runs operations in dependency order and in parallel where resources are independent (10 at a time by default, `-parallelism=N`). After a successful apply, a second apply with no code changes prints "No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.", which is the declarative model at work.

concepts.heading: -refresh-only, Drift and When Plans Differ
concepts.body: Suppose an engineer changes a tag on a load balancer in the console during an incident and the change should stay. Running a normal apply would revert it to the code. `terraform plan -refresh-only` shows how Terraform would update only its state records to match reality, without proposing any infrastructure change, and `terraform apply -refresh-only` writes that update. This is the supported replacement for the deprecated `terraform refresh` command, which wrote state with no review. After reconciling state you usually also update the configuration so the code describes the new reality, otherwise the next normal plan will want to change it back. The mirror case: if the console change was unwanted, a normal plan shows the drift as an update that restores the configuration. Reading a plan therefore means asking, for each line, whether it comes from your code change or from drift; both show up in the same output, which is why the plan is the review artifact.

examPoints: A question that asks for the way to apply exactly what reviewers approved points to terraform plan -out and terraform apply with that file, not to a second plain apply that would plan again.

A question about -target is testing that it limits the run to one resource and its dependencies, is meant for exceptions, and is not a regular workflow; planning options cannot be added to apply with a saved plan file.
A question where a console change should be kept in the record without Terraform reverting it is testing -refresh-only, which updates state only; refresh=false merely skips reading real objects.

quiz.q: A nightly job must fail only when the configuration and the real infrastructure differ, so on-call staff notice drift, and must stay green when there is nothing to change. Which command fits?
choices: terraform validate, which exits with a failure code whenever the real infrastructure no longer matches the files
terraform plan -detailed-exitcode, which exits with 2 when changes are present and 0 when the plan is empty
terraform plan -refresh=false, which exits with 1 whenever a resource in state differs from its cloud object
terraform apply -auto-approve, which exits with 2 whenever it had to correct any resource that changed
quiz.explain: -detailed-exitcode distinguishes empty (0), error (1) and changes (2), which is what a drift check needs. Choice A is tempting because it sounds like a check, but validate never contacts real infrastructure.

quiz.q: An engineer saves a plan with `terraform plan -out=tfplan`. A reviewer wants to read it before approving, without any risk of changing infrastructure. Which command is correct?
choices: terraform apply -refresh-only tfplan, which prints the plan and then asks before touching any resource
terraform validate tfplan, which checks the saved plan file and prints the proposed changes in order
terraform plan -out=tfplan again, which rewrites the file so that its contents are shown on the screen
terraform show tfplan, which renders the saved plan in readable form and applies nothing
quiz.explain: `terraform show` displays a saved plan without applying it. Choice A is tempting because refresh-only sounds read-only, but it is a different mode that writes state on approval and cannot take a plan file for a normal plan.

days.recap: Validate checks syntax, types and references offline after init; plan refreshes, compares and previews, in one mode per run, with -detailed-exitcode for automation and -target as an exception. Save with plan -out and apply the file to run exactly what was reviewed; use -refresh-only (not terraform refresh) to record outside changes.

days.title: destroy, fmt and Workflow Consolidation: -replace and Speculative Plans

concepts.heading: terraform destroy
concepts.body: `terraform destroy` removes the infrastructure that the state tracks. It is a shortcut for `terraform apply -destroy`: Terraform creates a destroy plan (every managed resource in reverse dependency order, so the instance goes before its subnet), shows it and asks for `yes`. Because it is an apply underneath, it also accepts `-auto-approve` and `-target`, but not a plan file argument. For a reviewed teardown, save a destroy plan and inspect it first: `terraform plan -destroy -out=destroy.tfplan`, read it with `terraform show destroy.tfplan`, then `terraform apply destroy.tfplan`. Destroy removes only what state tracks. A VM created by hand in the same subnet is not in state, so it survives; and if that VM blocks deletion of the subnet, the destroy fails on the subnet instead of removing the VM. Resources marked `prevent_destroy` in their lifecycle block make the plan fail rather than delete them, which protects a production database from an accidental destroy. After a successful destroy the state is empty but still exists.

concepts.heading: terraform fmt
concepts.body: `terraform fmt` rewrites configuration files to the canonical HCL style: two-space indentation, aligned equals signs in a block, consistent spacing. It changes only whitespace and layout, not meaning, so it is safe to run on every file. It prints the names of files it changed. By default it works on the current directory only; a `modules/` subfolder is untouched unless you add `-recursive`. In CI the options matter: `terraform fmt -check -recursive` exits with a non-zero status when any file is not formatted and writes nothing, so it can gate a pull request. `-diff` shows what would change, and `-write=false` stops it from modifying files, so `terraform fmt -diff -write=false` previews the edits for a reviewer. `-list=false` hides the file names. fmt does not validate: a file can be perfectly formatted and still reference an undefined variable, and it does not need init or credentials. Run it before commit so reviews show real changes rather than whitespace.

concepts.heading: Replacing a Resource with -replace
concepts.body: Sometimes a resource exists and matches its configuration but is broken: a VM that is misbehaving, a node that must be rebuilt. The supported way to force a rebuild is `terraform apply -replace="aws_instance.web"`, which plans to destroy and recreate that one instance (shown as `-/+`, "replace") even though no argument changed. You can also add `-replace` to `plan` to preview it. This replaces the deprecated `terraform taint` command, which marked a resource in state without a plan and review; `-replace` shows the effect in the plan before anything happens. Replacement order follows the resource's lifecycle: destroy then create by default, or create first with `create_before_destroy` (Day 10). A replacement can also be planned without your asking: when you change an argument that cannot be updated in place, the plan marks it "forces replacement", and that is the line to check carefully in review.

concepts.heading: Speculative Plans and Plans in HCP Terraform
concepts.body: In HCP Terraform, plans and applies can run remotely, and a plan-only run is called a speculative plan. It shows the possible changes (and checks them against policies) but Terraform cannot apply it, it does not take the workspace's run queue and it does not block other runs. They are created automatically when someone opens a pull request against the branch a VCS-connected workspace tracks, so reviewers see the effect of a change before merge, and a CLI-driven `terraform plan` against a workspace is also a speculative plan. The saved-plan idea is the same as locally: review first, then apply an approved plan; the difference is that in HCP Terraform the run, its logs and its state are stored for the team. You will meet runs and workspaces on Days 16 and 17; for Domain 3, remember that a speculative plan is safe to run anywhere because it can never be applied.

concepts.heading: Consolidating the Workflow: Which Command, When
concepts.body: A review table for the whole domain. Prepare a directory: `init` (backend, providers, modules). Check code: `fmt` for style, `validate` for syntax, types and references, both offline. Preview: `plan`, with `-out` to save, `-destroy` for teardown, `-refresh-only` to reconcile state, `-detailed-exitcode` for automation. Execute: `apply`, with a saved plan to run exactly what was reviewed, or `-auto-approve` where no one will review. Rebuild one object: `apply -replace=ADDR`. Tear down: `destroy` (or plan -destroy with -out). Inspect: `show` for state or a plan file. Deprecated commands to avoid in answers: `terraform refresh` (use `-refresh-only`) and `terraform taint` (use `-replace`). Typical confusions: validate versus plan (offline versus real), -migrate-state versus -reconfigure, -target as a habit versus an exception, and plan without -out being applied as reviewed. A fresh configuration in a pipeline runs: init, fmt -check, validate, plan -out, review, apply the saved plan.

examPoints: A question about running a formatting gate over all modules without modifying files is testing terraform fmt -check -recursive; plain fmt changes files and covers only the current directory.
A question where one misbehaving VM must be rebuilt without editing the configuration is testing apply -replace=ADDRESS, which replaces taint in the current workflow.
A question about a VM that survives destroy because it was created by hand is testing that Terraform destroys only what is in state, so unmanaged objects remain.

quiz.q: A CI job must block any pull request containing a .tf file in any subfolder that is not canonically formatted, and must leave the checked-out files unchanged. Which command satisfies both requirements?
choices: terraform fmt -recursive, which fails the job for unformatted files while leaving the rewritten files in the checkout
terraform validate -recursive, which fails the job for style problems found in every subfolder of the repository
terraform fmt -check, which covers every nested module directory by default and exits with a failure code
terraform fmt -check -recursive, which exits with a non-zero status for unformatted files and writes nothing
quiz.explain: -check reports without writing and -recursive extends it to subdirectories. Choice C is tempting because -check is the key flag, but without -recursive only the current directory is examined, and validate has no style rules at all.

quiz.q: A single aws_instance is healthy in the plan output but the operating system inside it is corrupted, and the team wants a fresh instance created from the same configuration, with the effect visible before it happens. What should the engineer run?
choices: terraform taint aws_instance.web, which marks the instance and shows the effect in the plan before anything changes
terraform plan -replace="aws_instance.web", then apply the same option to destroy and recreate only that instance
terraform apply -target=aws_instance.web, which destroys the targeted instance and always creates a new one
terraform init -upgrade, which rebuilds the resources whose providers changed since the last successful apply
quiz.explain: -replace previews and performs a destroy-and-create of the named resource. Choice A is tempting because taint did this job in older versions, but it is deprecated and changes state without a plan.

days.recap: destroy is apply -destroy and removes only what state tracks; save a destroy plan to review it. fmt -check -recursive gates style without writing, -replace rebuilds one object and replaces taint, and speculative plans in HCP Terraform preview changes but can never be applied.

days.title: Resource and Data Blocks, References, count and for_each

concepts.heading: Resource Blocks Manage, Data Blocks Read
concepts.body: A resource block describes an infrastructure object that Terraform manages: it creates it, updates it in place or replaces it, destroys it, and records it in state. A data block describes an object that already exists and that Terraform only reads. It never creates or deletes anything, so removing a data block from the configuration leaves the real object untouched. Typical lookups are an AMI, a VPC built by another team or the current account ID. The arguments of a data block are filters such as an ID, a name or a tag, and the attributes it returns are used by other blocks. Example: `data "aws_vpc" "shared" { tags = { Name = "shared-network" } }` lets subnets use `data.aws_vpc.shared.id` without Terraform ever owning the VPC. A data source is read at plan time when its arguments are already known, and the read is deferred to apply time when an argument depends on a value that does not exist yet. Declaring a second resource block for an existing object is not a lookup: it plans to create a new one. Bringing an existing object under management is an import, which is a different feature.

concepts.heading: Resource Addresses and Naming
concepts.body: Every managed resource has an address made of its type and its local name, such as `aws_s3_bucket.logs`. Data sources use the same shape with a `data.` prefix: `data.aws_ami.ubuntu`. The local name only has to be unique among blocks of the same type in the same module, and it is private to the configuration; it is not the name of the real object in the cloud. That is why `aws_s3_bucket.logs` and `aws_s3_bucket_versioning.logs` can coexist, because the type is part of the address. Two blocks with the same type and name in one module produce a duplicate-resource error. The address matters beyond naming: state records objects by address, and commands such as `-replace`, `-target` and `terraform state show` take addresses. Renaming a block without telling Terraform looks like a destroy of the old address and a create of the new one, which is the problem the moved block (Domain 6) solves. Block order across files does not matter, because Terraform reads all `.tf` files in the directory and builds the graph from references.

concepts.heading: References and Implicit Dependencies
concepts.body: When an argument refers to an attribute of another object, Terraform adds an edge to its dependency graph. A server with `vpc_security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.web.id]` is created after the group and destroyed before it, with no extra syntax. The syntax is `<TYPE>.<NAME>.<ATTRIBUTE>` for resources, `data.<TYPE>.<NAME>.<ATTRIBUTE>` for data sources, `var.<NAME>` for inputs, `local.<NAME>` for locals and `module.<LABEL>.<OUTPUT>` for module outputs. Attributes that are only known after creation, such as an ID or a generated IP address, are shown as `(known after apply)` in the plan, and anything that uses them is also unknown until apply. Objects with no path between them in the graph are processed in parallel, by default up to 10 operations at once. The explicit `depends_on` meta-argument exists only for hidden dependencies that no reference can express (Day 10), so prefer a reference whenever an attribute can carry the relationship. Destroy runs the same graph in reverse: dependents go first, dependencies last.

concepts.heading: count: N Copies or an On/Off Switch
concepts.body: The count meta-argument takes a whole number and creates that many instances of a resource, module or data block. Instances are addressed by position, `aws_subnet.main[0]`, `[1]` and so on, and `count.index` gives the current number inside the block. The most common idiom is a switch: `count = var.enable_backup ? 1 : 0` creates one bucket or none, because a block has no `if` argument. References to a counted resource need an index (`aws_s3_bucket.backup[0].id`) or a splat such as `aws_s3_bucket.backup[*].id`, which returns a list that is empty when the count is 0. The weakness of count is identity by position. If subnets are built with `count = length(var.cidrs)` and `cidr_block = var.cidrs[count.index]`, removing the first entry shifts every later item down one index, so the plan changes the remaining instances and destroys the last index although only one subnet should disappear. Use count for identical copies or on/off; use for_each when each instance is a distinct item that may come and go.

concepts.heading: for_each: Instances Keyed by Name
concepts.body: The for_each meta-argument takes a map or a set of strings and creates one instance per key. Instances are addressed by key, `aws_iam_user.staff["bob"]`, and inside the block `each.key` and `each.value` name the current element (for a set both are the same string). A list is not accepted directly because it may hold duplicates and has no natural keys, so convert it: `for_each = toset(var.names)`. Removing a key affects only that instance, which is why a stable map solves the shifting problem of count. Rules to remember: count and for_each cannot be used on the same block; the keys must be known during planning, although values may be unknown, so keys cannot depend on an attribute that only exists after apply; and `each.value` is not available from other blocks. To read one attribute from every instance, a resource with for_each is a map of objects, so use a for expression, `[for u in aws_iam_user.staff : u.arn]`, because the splat `[*]` does not apply to maps. Both meta-arguments also work on module blocks.

examPoints: A data block only reads an existing object and never creates or deletes it; a resource block with the same details would try to create a new one.
Referencing another object's attribute creates an implicit dependency; use depends_on only when no reference can express the ordering.
for_each needs a map or a set of strings (use toset() on lists), is addressed by key, and cannot be combined with count on the same block.

quiz.q: A team must attach a new instance to an AMI that another pipeline publishes and tags with Name = "golden-base". Terraform must not create, modify or delete that AMI. Which configuration is correct?
choices: A resource "aws_ami" "golden" block with the same tags, so Terraform adopts the image the next time it plans
A data "aws_ami" "golden" block that filters on the Name tag, then ami = data.aws_ami.golden.id in the instance
A locals block that calls the AWS API with the tag filter and stores the returned image ID for the instance
A variable "golden" with a type constraint of string that Terraform fills by querying the account at plan time
quiz.explain: A data block reads an existing object through the provider and exposes its attributes under data.<TYPE>.<NAME>, with no management of the object itself. A resource block would plan to create a second image, locals cannot call provider APIs, and a variable only receives values from the caller.

quiz.q: A resource uses for_each = toset(["web", "api", "batch"]). A reviewer wants an output with the IDs of all three instances as a list. Which expression works?
choices: aws_instance.svc[*].id, a splat written directly on the resource
aws_instance.svc.id, an attribute read without choosing a key
values(aws_instance.svc)[*].id, converting the map to a list first
aws_instance.svc[0..2].id, a range over the three instances
quiz.explain: A for_each resource is a map of instances keyed by name, so the plain splat does not apply to it; values() turns the map into a list and the splat then extracts id (a for expression such as [for i in aws_instance.svc : i.id] is equivalent). Attribute access without a key and range syntax are not valid.

days.recap: Resource blocks manage and data blocks only read. References build the graph and order work. count identifies instances by position (good for on/off switches), for_each by key (good for distinct items); for_each takes a map or set of strings and is not combinable with count.

days.title: Input Variables, Outputs and Complex Types

concepts.heading: Declaring Input Variables
concepts.body: A variable block declares an input of a module. Its useful arguments are `type`, `default`, `description`, `nullable`, `sensitive`, `ephemeral` and `validation`. A variable without a default is required: Terraform prompts for it when a run is interactive, and fails with an error naming the variable when input is disabled (`-input=false`, typical in CI). Setting a default makes the variable optional. Variables are referenced as `var.<NAME>` and, in the root module, are the only way to parameterize a configuration from outside. Values are not remembered in state, so every run needs all values again from one of the sources on the precedence list. In a child module the inputs are set only as arguments in the `module` block; `-var`, `-var-file`, tfvars files and TF_VAR_ variables apply to the root module alone. Example: `variable "instance_type" { type = string }` becomes optional once a `default = "t3.micro"` line is added inside the block. A type constraint makes Terraform reject or convert wrong values early; without one the type is `any`. Conversions that are safe are applied automatically, for instance the string "5" to the number 5.

concepts.heading: Variable Precedence
concepts.body: When several sources set the same variable, the later and higher one wins. From lowest to highest: the `default` in the variable block; environment variables named `TF_VAR_<name>`; `terraform.tfvars`; `terraform.tfvars.json`; `*.auto.tfvars` and `*.auto.tfvars.json` in lexical order; and `-var` and `-var-file` on the command line, in the order they are written, which is the highest tier (values set in an HCP Terraform workspace also take part in this top tier). So with a default of t3.micro, a terraform.tfvars of t3.small, an auto.tfvars of t3.medium and TF_VAR_instance_type=t3.large exported, a plain apply uses t3.medium. The command-line options share one tier and are applied in order: `-var="region=eu-west-1" -var-file=prod.tfvars` ends with the region from the file, while reversing them ends with eu-west-1. Terraform loads terraform.tfvars and *.auto.tfvars automatically; any other file, such as prod.tfvars, is used only when passed with `-var-file`. Setting the same variable twice inside one file is an error.

concepts.heading: Validation and Optional Attributes
concepts.body: Type constraints check shape, not allowed values. To restrict values, add a validation block inside the variable, with a `condition` that must be true and an `error_message` string, for example `condition = contains(["dev", "stage", "prod"], var.env)`. Terraform evaluates it when it processes inputs at the start of a plan, so a bad value stops the run before any resource is planned. A variable may hold several validation blocks. Object types can mark attributes optional with a default: `object({ protocol = string, port = optional(number, 8080) })`. A caller that passes only `{ protocol = "HTTPS" }` gets port 8080 filled in, and a caller that sets port keeps it. Without the second argument an omitted optional attribute becomes null. Every attribute not wrapped in optional() is required. With `nullable = false` the variable can never hold null: an explicit null from the caller is replaced by the default, or is an error when there is no default. Together, types, optional attributes and validation make a module interface that fails early and clearly.

concepts.heading: Collection and Structural Types
concepts.body: Terraform has primitive types (string, number, bool) and two families of complex types. Collections hold many values of one type: `list(T)` is ordered and indexed from 0, `set(T)` is unordered with unique values and no index, and `map(T)` has string keys with all values of type T. Structural types hold values of different types: `object({ name = string, cpu_count = number, tags = list(string) })` has named attributes that each carry their own type, and `tuple([string, number, bool])` has a fixed number of positions with individual types. A record with a string, a number and a list is the standard case for an object; a map(string) could not carry the list. A list(object({...})) models many such records, and a map(object({...})) is the natural input for for_each. The keyword `any` lets Terraform infer a single concrete type, but it does not permit mixed element types inside one list. Converting between types uses functions such as toset(), tolist(), tomap() and tostring(). Choosing the right type makes validation, defaults and for_each work with the least code.

concepts.heading: Output Values
concepts.body: An output block exposes a value from a module. In the root module, outputs are printed at the end of apply and stored in state, so they can be read later with `terraform output`. Useful forms: `terraform output` lists all outputs, `terraform output NAME` shows one, `terraform output -json` prints JSON (strings keep their quotes), and `terraform output -raw NAME` prints a bare string, number or bool with no quotes or newline, which suits scripts: `terraform output -raw lb_dns`. An output takes `value`, `description`, `sensitive` and `depends_on`, and may hold a precondition (Day 10). In a child module, outputs are the only way to return values to the caller, read as `module.<LABEL>.<OUTPUT>`. The command `terraform output` lists only root outputs, so to show a child value to a user or to a configuration that reads this state, re-export it: `output "vpc_id" { value = module.network.vpc_id }`. Outputs marked sensitive are redacted in normal CLI output but remain readable with -raw and -json, a point Day 11 expands.

examPoints: Variable precedence from lowest to highest: default, TF_VAR_ environment, terraform.tfvars, *.auto.tfvars, then -var and -var-file in the order given.
A validation block with condition and error_message checks allowed values during plan; a type constraint checks only shape, and optional(type, default) gives object attributes a default.
Collections hold one type (list, set, map); structural types mix types (object with named attributes, tuple with positions); terraform output -raw prints a bare value for scripts.

quiz.q: The shell exports TF_VAR_zone=eu-west-1a. The directory has terraform.tfvars (zone = "eu-west-1b") and a file ops.tfvars (zone = "eu-west-1c"), and the variable default is "eu-west-1d". A teammate runs terraform apply with no options. Which zone is used?
choices: eu-west-1a, because environment variables are read last and therefore override every tfvars file
eu-west-1c, because the newest tfvars file in the working directory is always loaded as well
eu-west-1d, because the default in the variable block always wins in the root module
eu-west-1b, because terraform.tfvars loads automatically and outranks the environment and default
quiz.explain: terraform.tfvars is loaded automatically and ranks above TF_VAR_ variables and the default. ops.tfvars is not an automatic name (only terraform.tfvars and *.auto.tfvars are), so it is ignored unless passed with -var-file.

quiz.q: A module needs a variable named retry that is an object with a required string attribute mode and an attribute attempts that defaults to 3 when omitted. Which type constraint is correct?
choices: map(string) with a default of { attempts = 3 }
tuple([string, number]) with validation that the second element is 3
object({ mode = string, attempts = optional(number, 3) })
list(any) with a default of ["fixed", 3] for both entries
quiz.explain: An object type gives named attributes with their own types, and optional(number, 3) makes attempts optional with a default. A map cannot hold a number next to a string type-safely, a tuple has positions not names, and list(any) cannot mix element types.

days.recap: Variables get values by precedence (default lowest, -var and -var-file highest, applied in order). Use type, validation and optional() for a safe interface. Know list, set, map versus object and tuple. Outputs leave a module; terraform output -raw is for scripts.

days.title: Expressions, Functions, Conditionals, for Expressions, Splat and Dynamic Blocks

concepts.heading: Locals and Built-in Functions
concepts.body: A locals block names an expression so it can be reused as `local.<NAME>`: `locals { default_tags = { env = "dev", owner = "platform" } }`. Locals compute values from other values; they do not read provider data and are private to the module. Terraform has many built-in functions and no way to define your own. Common ones: `merge(m1, m2)` combines maps and the later argument wins on a duplicate key, so `merge(local.default_tags, var.extra_tags)` applies defaults and lets callers override single keys; `concat()` joins lists and `flatten()` removes nesting; `lookup(map, key, default)` reads a key with a fallback; `join()` and `split()` convert between lists and strings, and `split` returns a list; `format("%03d", 7)` gives "007"; `length()`, `keys()`, `values()` and `toset()` are everyday helpers. `element(list, index)` wraps around, so index 4 on three items returns the second item. `cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 2)` adds 8 bits to the prefix and picks subnet number 2, giving "10.0.2.0/24". `terraform console` lets you try any of these interactively.

concepts.heading: Conditional Expressions
concepts.body: A conditional has the form `condition ? true_value : false_value`. The condition must be a bool and both results should be of compatible types. Terraform has no `if` argument on a resource block, so a conditional is used in two ways: as a value, `instance_type = var.env == "prod" ? "m5.large" : "t3.micro"`, or as a switch on count, `count = var.enable_backup ? 1 : 0`, which creates one instance or none. Once a resource uses count, other blocks reference it with an index or splat, such as `aws_s3_bucket.backup[0].id`, or `one(aws_s3_bucket.backup[*].id)` to get a single value or null. Conditionals combine with the comparison operators (`==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`), the logical operators (`&&`, `||`, `!`) and functions such as `contains()` and `can()`. The two results must be convertible to one type, so keep both branches simple; when a branch refers to something that may not exist, prefer try(), one() or a count switch over a nested conditional.

concepts.heading: for Expressions
concepts.body: A for expression transforms or filters a collection and builds a new one. Square brackets produce a list (a tuple): `[for s in var.servers : s.name]`. Curly braces produce a map (an object) and use `=>` between key and value: `{ for k, v in var.sizes : k => upper(v) }`. An optional `if` clause at the end filters: `[for s in var.servers : s.name if s.enabled]` returns the names of only the enabled servers. There is no `where` keyword. With two iterator names a for expression over a list gives index and element, and over a map gives key and value. The input can be a list, set, map, tuple or object. For expressions are the standard way to read attributes from every instance of a for_each resource, because that resource is a map of objects: `[for i in aws_instance.web : i.private_ip]`. They also reshape data to feed other features, for example turning a list of objects into a map keyed by name so it can drive for_each: `{ for s in var.servers : s.name => s }`. Adding `...` after the value expression groups values under duplicate keys into lists, which is rarely needed.

concepts.heading: Splat Expressions
concepts.body: A splat expression is a short form for extracting one attribute from every element of a list, set or tuple. `aws_instance.web[*].private_ip` is the same as `[for o in aws_instance.web : o.private_ip]`. It fits resources created with count, which are lists of instances, and module calls with count. It does not apply to a resource with for_each, which appears as a map of objects, so use a for expression there, or `values(aws_instance.web)[*].private_ip`. The splat has a second behavior that is useful with optional resources: applied to a single value that might be null, it returns an empty list for null and a one-element list otherwise, which is why `one(var.website[*])` can turn an optional value into zero or one items. A resource with count 0 is already an empty list, so `aws_s3_bucket.backup[*].id` is empty and `one()` returns null. The legacy attribute-only form `.*` exists, but `[*]` is the form to write. Splat is for simple extraction only; when you need filtering or transformation, use a full for expression.

concepts.heading: Dynamic Blocks
concepts.body: Some resources have repeatable nested blocks, such as `ingress` in a security group. Inside a nested block you cannot use count or for_each, so Terraform provides the dynamic block, which generates one nested block per element of a collection. Example: a `dynamic "ingress"` block with `for_each = var.ports` and a `content` block that sets `from_port = ingress.value`. The label ("ingress") is the type of nested block to generate. Inside content, a temporary variable named after the label holds the current element, with `.key` and `.value`; the optional `iterator` argument renames that variable. The expression `each.value` belongs to resource-level for_each and is not available there. Dynamic blocks generate nested blocks only; they cannot create top-level blocks such as resources. Overuse makes configuration hard to read, so reach for a dynamic block only when the number of nested blocks truly depends on input, and write literal blocks when the list is fixed.

examPoints: merge() lets the later map win on duplicate keys, element() wraps around by index, and cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 2) returns 10.0.2.0/24.

A for expression uses [ ] for lists and { k => v } for maps, filters with a trailing if, and is the way to read attributes from a for_each resource; the [*] splat works on lists such as count instances.
A dynamic block generates repeated nested blocks from a collection and exposes the current element as <label>.value inside content.

quiz.q: A security group must get one egress rule for every CIDR string in var.cidrs. A literal egress block is written once and the team wants to loop over the list. Which construct is correct?
choices: A dynamic "egress" block with for_each = var.cidrs, reading egress.value inside content
An egress block with count = length(var.cidrs) and count.index used inside the block
An egress block with for_each = toset(var.cidrs) and each.value used inside the block
A for expression wrapped around the whole security group resource block definition
quiz.explain: Nested blocks cannot take count or for_each, so the dynamic block generates one per element and exposes the element as <label>.value (egress.value). each.value belongs to resource-level for_each.

quiz.q: local.nodes is a map such as { a = "10.0.1.5", b = "10.0.1.6" }. Which expression returns the list of IP values whose key is not "b"?
choices: [for v in local.nodes : v where v != "b"]
local.nodes[*].v where k != "b"
[for k, v in local.nodes : v if k != "b"]
{ for k, v in local.nodes : k => v if k != "b" }
quiz.explain: Square brackets build a list, two iterator names give key and value, and the trailing if filters. Curly braces would return a map, and Terraform has no where keyword or filtering splat.

days.recap: locals name expressions; merge, element, cidrsubnet and friends are built in (no user functions). cond ? a : b plus count gives optional resources. for builds lists with [ ] and maps with { => }; splat handles count lists; dynamic generates nested blocks.

days.title: depends_on, Lifecycle Rules and Custom Conditions

concepts.heading: depends_on for Hidden Dependencies
concepts.body: Terraform orders work from references. Sometimes a dependency exists but no argument expresses it. For example an instance runs a bootstrap script that needs an IAM policy already attached to its role, the instance refers only to the instance profile, and the policy attachment is a separate resource nobody refers to. The graph has no edge, so the two may be created in parallel and the script sometimes fails. The depends_on meta-argument takes a list of resources or modules and adds an explicit edge: `depends_on = [aws_iam_role_policy_attachment.app]`. The resource then waits for everything listed and is destroyed before them. It works on resources, data sources, modules and outputs. Use it only for hidden dependencies, because it makes Terraform plan more conservatively, which can show more pending changes than a precise reference would. Whenever an attribute can carry the relationship, use the reference instead. On a module block, depends_on is a direct meta-argument, not nested inside lifecycle.

concepts.heading: create_before_destroy
concepts.body: When an argument cannot be updated in place, Terraform replaces the object. By default it destroys the old object and then creates the new one. In the lifecycle block, `create_before_destroy = true` reverses that order: the replacement is built first and the old object is removed afterwards, which avoids downtime for things other objects depend on. It is opt-in because the remote system must tolerate two objects existing at once. A security group with a fixed `name` collides with itself during replacement and the apply fails with an error that the name already exists; the fix is to give each copy a distinct name, for example with `name_prefix`. The setting propagates to dependencies: if A has it and depends on B, Terraform enables it for B implicitly, and B cannot override it to false because that would imply a dependency cycle. It does not turn a replacement into an in-place update. Enabling it also prevents a destroy-time provisioner from running, a detail that appears in exam options.

concepts.heading: prevent_destroy and ignore_changes
concepts.body: Two more lifecycle arguments protect configuration from surprises. `prevent_destroy = true` makes Terraform stop with an error for any plan that would destroy the resource, which guards a database or bucket from an accidental replacement or terraform destroy. It is not a lock on the real object: if you delete the whole resource block from the configuration the protection disappears with it, and anyone can still delete the object outside Terraform. `ignore_changes = [tags]` tells Terraform to ignore differences in the listed arguments after creation, which suits attributes that another system modifies, such as tags added by a policy tool or an autoscaler changing a desired size. The value is a list of argument names (the special keyword `all` ignores every argument). Terraform still applies the configured value on creation; it just stops treating later drift in that argument as a change. Overusing ignore_changes hides real drift, so keep the list short. For a one-off rebuild use `-replace`, not lifecycle settings.

concepts.heading: Preconditions and Postconditions
concepts.body: Custom conditions (Terraform 1.2 and later) put assumptions and guarantees next to the objects they concern. A precondition is tested before Terraform plans or creates the object and checks assumptions about inputs or other objects, such as the chosen AMI having the expected architecture. It cannot use `self`, because the object does not exist yet. A postcondition is tested after the object is planned or read and checks guarantees, and `self` refers to the object itself, as in `condition = self.public_ip != ""` inside a postcondition block that also carries an `error_message`. Both live in the lifecycle block of resource and data blocks, and an output block accepts precondition directly. A false condition stops the operation with the error_message. Variable validation, from Day 8, checks one input at the start of the plan. Choose by what you must read: only the input, validation; assumptions before building, precondition; results after building, postcondition. A failing postcondition on a managed resource happens after the object was created, so the run fails but the object may exist.

concepts.heading: check Blocks
concepts.body: A check block (Terraform 1.5 and later) validates infrastructure without blocking the run. It is a top-level block holding optional scoped data sources and one or more assert blocks, each with a condition and an error_message. Terraform evaluates checks at the end of plan and apply; when an assertion is false it reports a warning and carries on, so the run still finishes. Example: a `check "site_health"` block holds a scoped `data "http" "site"` source and an `assert` block with `condition = data.http.site.status_code == 200` and an `error_message`. The data source declared inside the check is scoped to it and cannot be referenced elsewhere, and failures in it are also downgraded to warnings. This is the right feature for health tests such as "the site responds after apply"; if a failure should stop the run, use a precondition or postcondition. HCP Terraform can run checks continuously as health assessments. Summary of where conditions live: validation in variables, pre/postconditions in lifecycle blocks and outputs, assert in check blocks.

examPoints: depends_on adds an explicit edge for hidden dependencies only; create_before_destroy builds the replacement first, needs distinct names, and propagates to dependencies.
prevent_destroy errors on any plan that would destroy the resource, ignore_changes stops listed arguments from counting as changes, and neither replaces -replace.
Precondition runs before and cannot use self, postcondition runs after and can, and a check block with assert only warns and never stops the run.

quiz.q: An autoscaling tool changes the desired_capacity argument of an aws_autoscaling_group every hour. Each terraform plan then proposes to reset it to the value in the configuration. The team wants Terraform to create the group with the configured value but stop reverting later changes to that argument. What should they do?
choices: Add prevent_destroy = true to the lifecycle block so the group cannot be modified
Add depends_on = [aws_autoscaling_policy.scale] so the tool runs before every plan
Set create_before_destroy = true so the changed group is rebuilt before the old one goes
Add lifecycle { ignore_changes = [desired_capacity] } to the group
