quiz.explain: ignore_changes lists arguments whose later differences Terraform ignores while still using the configured value at creation. prevent_destroy only blocks destruction, depends_on affects ordering, and create_before_destroy changes replacement order.

quiz.q: A team wants every deployment of an aws_db_instance to fail when the engine version reported by the created database does not start with "16". Which feature expresses this?
choices: A check block with an assert, which stops the run when the condition is false
A postcondition in the lifecycle block using self.engine_version in the condition
A precondition in the lifecycle block using self.engine_version in the condition
A validation block in the variable that names the engine version
quiz.explain: The test reads an attribute of the object after it exists, and it must fail the run, which is what a postcondition with self does. A precondition cannot use self, a check block only warns, and variable validation only sees the input, not what the provider reports.

days.recap: depends_on is for hidden dependencies; lifecycle holds create_before_destroy (opt-in, propagates), prevent_destroy (error on destroy plans) and ignore_changes. Pre and postconditions stop the run, with self only in postconditions; check blocks warn without stopping.

days.title: Sensitive Values, Ephemeral Values, Write-Only Arguments and Vault; Domain 4 Review

concepts.heading: What sensitive Does and Does Not Do
concepts.body: Setting `sensitive = true` on a variable or output tells Terraform to redact the value in CLI output, printing `(sensitive value)`, and in the HCP Terraform UI. Any expression that uses a sensitive value is treated as sensitive too, so the flag spreads through locals and resources that reference it. This is a display feature only. The value is still stored in plain text in the state file and in saved plan files, and `terraform output -json` or `terraform output -raw NAME` print it. A colleague who says a marked password can no longer leak is wrong: anyone who can read the state can read the password. Protecting it takes encrypted remote state with tight access control. A sensitive value also cannot be used where Terraform would have to show it, such as a for_each argument, without wrapping it deliberately with `nonsensitive()`, which you should use only when you know the value is safe to expose. Sensitive hides; it does not remove.

concepts.heading: Ephemeral Variables and Resources
concepts.body: Terraform 1.10 introduced ephemeral values, which exist only for the current operation and are never written to state or plan files. A variable can be declared `ephemeral = true`, and an `ephemeral` block declares a temporary object such as a generated password or a secret read from a vault: `ephemeral "random_password" "db" { length = 16 }`. It is referenced as `ephemeral.<TYPE>.<NAME>.<ATTRIBUTE>`. Because nothing is stored, Terraform restricts where such a value can flow. It may be used in locals, in variables or child-module outputs that are themselves ephemeral, in write-only arguments of managed resources, in other ephemeral blocks, in provider blocks and in provisioner and connection blocks. Using it in an ordinary resource argument would require writing it to state, so Terraform stops with an error at plan time. Ephemeral can be combined with sensitive to redact the value in the CLI and UI as well. Typical uses are credentials for a provider block and passwords handed to a database resource without persisting them.

concepts.heading: Write-Only Arguments
concepts.body: Write-only arguments came in Terraform 1.11. A write-only argument, whose name usually ends in `_wo`, is an argument on a managed resource that accepts a value and sends it to the provider but is never stored in state or in the plan. Support depends on the provider and resource. Because Terraform keeps no copy, it cannot see whether the value changed, so such arguments come with a companion version argument, for example `password_wo_version`; raising the number tells Terraform that the value changed and must be sent again. A complete pattern: `ephemeral "random_password" "db" { length = 16 }` and then an `aws_db_instance` that sets `password_wo = ephemeral.random_password.db.result` and `password_wo_version = 1`. The password never appears in state. Remember the pairing: an ephemeral value is the source, a write-only argument is the sink that may receive it, and the version argument is how you rotate. A regular argument such as password would be rejected for an ephemeral value because it would be persisted.

concepts.heading: Secrets with HashiCorp Vault
concepts.body: HashiCorp Vault is a secrets manager, and Terraform integrates with it through the Vault provider, which authenticates to Vault and reads or writes secrets. A strong pattern is dynamic secrets: a Vault secrets engine, for example the AWS secrets engine, creates credentials on demand with a limited scope and a time to live (TTL), the configuration reads them and passes them to the cloud provider, and Vault revokes them when the lease ends. Operators no longer keep long-lived static access keys in CI variables, a leaked credential works only until the TTL expires, and developers can provision without direct access to the secret. The caveat is state: values read through ordinary data sources are still stored in state, so secure the state with encrypted remote storage and access control, or use ephemeral resources where the provider offers them so the secret is not persisted. Related defaults: never commit secrets into configuration or tfvars files in version control, and prefer environment variables or a secrets store for provider credentials.

concepts.heading: Domain 4 Consolidation
concepts.body: Domain 4 asks you to predict what Terraform does with a configuration, so rehearse the pairings. Resource versus data: manage versus read. count versus for_each: position versus key, and a map or set of strings for for_each. Variable precedence: default, TF_VAR_, terraform.tfvars, auto.tfvars, then command-line options in the order given. Types: list, set and map hold one type; object and tuple mix types. Expressions: conditional with count for optional resources, for with [ ] or { }, splat for counted lists, dynamic blocks for repeated nested blocks. Dependencies: references first, depends_on for hidden ones. Lifecycle: create_before_destroy, prevent_destroy, ignore_changes. Conditions: validation for inputs, precondition before, postcondition after, check only warns. Secrets: sensitive hides output only, ephemeral plus write-only keeps values out of state, Vault supplies short-lived credentials. When an option says a flag keeps a value out of the state file, check whether it is sensitive (it does not) or ephemeral with a write-only sink (it does).

examPoints: sensitive = true redacts CLI and UI output but the value stays in plain text in state and plan files, and output -raw or -json still prints it.

Ephemeral variables and resources are never stored in state, can flow only into places such as write-only arguments, locals and provider blocks, and a write-only argument is rotated by raising its _wo_version.
Vault dynamic secrets give short-lived credentials revoked after their TTL, but values read by ordinary data sources still land in state.

quiz.q: A configuration sets password = random_password.db.result on an aws_db_instance and marks the output that echoes it as sensitive = true. An auditor finds the password on disk. Where is it, and what keeps it out next time?
choices: In the plan output only; adding -compact-warnings to later runs keeps it out of the logs
In the provider cache under .terraform; running terraform init -upgrade rewrites the cache without it
In the state file in plain text; use an ephemeral resource with a write-only argument such as password_wo
In the dependency lock file; deleting .terraform.lock.hcl and running init again removes the value
quiz.explain: sensitive only redacts display, so the generated and applied value is stored in state. An ephemeral block feeding a write-only argument keeps it out of state and plan files. The provider cache and lock file do not store resource values.

quiz.q: A variable declared with ephemeral = true is referenced in the arguments below. Which use is accepted by Terraform 1.12?
choices: The ordinary engine_version argument of an aws_db_instance resource
The name argument of a resource whose value is stored in state
The key expression of a for_each on a managed resource
The configuration of a provider block, for example a token argument
quiz.explain: Ephemeral values may flow into provider blocks, locals, write-only arguments, other ephemeral blocks and provisioner or connection blocks. Ordinary resource arguments and for_each keys would be persisted in state, so Terraform returns an error.

days.recap: sensitive hides output only; ephemeral values never reach state and may flow only into write-only arguments, locals, provider blocks and similar. Raise _wo_version to rotate. Vault gives short-lived dynamic credentials, but data source results still land in state.

days.title: Modules: Sources, Versions, Inputs and Outputs, Scope and Composition

concepts.heading: Module Sources
concepts.body: A module is a set of .tf files in one directory; the directory you run Terraform in is the root module, and every module block calls a child module. The `source` argument is a literal string, and Terraform decides what kind of location it is from how the string starts. `./` or `../` is a local path relative to the calling module, loaded from the same repository and so always at the caller's version: `source = "./modules/vpc"`. A three-part address `hashicorp/consul/aws` is the public Terraform Registry, in the form <NAMESPACE>/<NAME>/<PROVIDER>. A private registry adds a host in front: `app.terraform.io/example-corp/k8s-cluster/azurerm` for an HCP Terraform organization. Prefixes such as `git::`, `s3::` and `gcs::` select remote locations, for example `git::https://example.com/vpc.git?ref=v1.2.0`. A double slash marks a sub-directory inside a package: `git::https://example.com/network.git//modules/vpc?ref=v1.2.0`, with query parameters after the path. For S3 and GCS the object must be an archive such as .zip or .tar.gz, and credentials come from the usual environment variables or default profiles, never from the module block.

concepts.heading: Installing Modules and Pinning Versions
concepts.body: Module code is downloaded during `terraform init`, which scans the module blocks and places each source in a hidden subdirectory of the working directory under `.terraform`. Later plan and apply runs use that local copy, so they stop with an error if modules were never installed. `terraform get` downloads and updates only modules, useful when nothing else needs initializing. Re-running init installs only modules added since the last run unless you pass `-upgrade`. Changing a module's source, or the version of a registry module, makes the copy out of date and requires init again; changing input values, count, for_each or depends_on does not. The `version` argument works only for registry modules (public or private), because only registries can list and select versions. It uses the same constraint syntax as providers: `~> 4.2.0` allows 4.2.x only, while `~> 4.2` allows anything from 4.2 up to below 5.0. For Git sources, pin with `?ref=`: a branch can move, a tag can be moved by a maintainer, and a full commit SHA identifies one exact snapshot. Local modules do not support the version argument.

concepts.heading: Inputs, Outputs and Scope
concepts.body: Each module has its own scope. Its variables, locals and resources exist only inside it, and nothing flows in unless passed explicitly. Parent to child: arguments in the module block set the child's declared input variables, as in an extra line `size = var.size` inside the `module "app"` block. A child that uses `var.region` without declaring it fails with a reference to an undeclared input variable, even if the root declares the same name. A child variable without a default is required and omitting it is a "missing required argument" error. Command-line `-var`, tfvars files and TF_VAR_ variables reach only root module variables, so to set a child input from the command line, declare a root variable and pass it down. Child to parent: output blocks, read as `module.<LABEL>.<OUTPUT>`; resources inside the child are invisible to the caller unless exposed. The built-in module-block arguments are source, version, count, for_each, providers and depends_on; any other argument is an input, and an unknown name is an error. `terraform output` shows root outputs only, so re-export a child value in the root if people or scripts need it.

concepts.heading: Calling Modules Repeatedly and Ordering
concepts.body: A module is a template that you can call many times, each call with its own label and inputs, such as a small and a large web tier built from the same ./modules/web. Resources land at addresses like `module.web_small.aws_instance.this`, and nested calls extend the path (`module.app.module.db.aws_instance.primary`). Labels must be unique within the calling module. For variations of one list or map, put count or for_each on the module block, which has worked since Terraform 0.13. With for_each over a set, the call is a map keyed by the elements, so the output is read as `module.site["green"].url`; with count it is a list, `module.cache[0].endpoint`, and `module.cache[*].endpoint` collects all of them, empty when the count is 0. Count and for_each are mutually exclusive on one block. Ordering follows references: `subnet_ids = module.network.private_subnet_ids` makes the database module wait for the network. When there is a real dependency but no value is passed, add `depends_on = [aws_s3_bucket.logs]` to the module block. Removing a module block plans to destroy everything it created; to keep the real objects, use a removed block with `lifecycle { destroy = false }`.

concepts.heading: Composition and Publishing
concepts.body: HashiCorp recommends a flat module tree with one level of child modules, wired together in the calling module with expressions. A consul cluster module takes `vpc_id` and `subnet_ids` as inputs, filled from a network module's outputs, so the cluster does not care how the VPC was made and the VPC could later come from a data source. Conditional creation is handled by the caller passing the object in rather than the module testing for it. A good module describes a new concept built from several resources, such as a Consul cluster in AWS, and hides detail behind a small interface. A thin wrapper around a single resource type that passes every argument through adds a layer without new abstraction and is discouraged; use the resource directly. To publish to the public Terraform Registry, the repository must be public on GitHub, be named `terraform-<PROVIDER>-<NAME>`, and carry at least one release tag that is a semantic version, optionally prefixed with v. A new release is a new tag. The public GitHub requirement applies only to the public registry; private registries in HCP Terraform and Terraform Enterprise are covered on Day 16.

examPoints: source tells Terraform where a module lives (./ local, <NAMESPACE>/<NAME>/<PROVIDER> registry, git::, s3::, gcs::), and version works only for registry modules; pin Git with ?ref=, ideally a commit SHA.
A module has its own scope: values go in only through module block arguments and come out only through outputs, and -var or tfvars reach root variables only.

terraform init installs modules into .terraform and must be rerun after changing source or version; count and for_each work on module blocks, and flat composition with small interfaces is the recommended design.

quiz.q: An engineer runs terraform apply -var="instance_size=large". The value is declared only in ./modules/web as variable "instance_size", and Terraform reports an undeclared variable. What is the correct fix?
choices: Declare variable "instance_size" in the root module and set instance_size = var.instance_size in the module block
Move the variable declaration into a terraform.tfvars file so the child module reads it automatically on every run
Add the argument -target=module.web to the command so the command-line value is routed into the child module
Rename the child variable to TF_VAR_instance_size so the environment passes it into the module without arguments
quiz.explain: Command-line values, tfvars files and TF_VAR_ variables target root module variables only. A child input is set as an argument in the module block, so the root variable must exist and be passed down. A tfvars file does not declare variables, and -target selects resources.

quiz.q: A team calls a module published as vendor/queue/aws in the public registry with version = "~> 2.4". The registry offers 2.3.9, 2.4.0, 2.7.2, 3.0.0. Nothing is installed yet. Which version does terraform init install, and what is needed to later move to 3.0.0?
choices: 2.4.0; run terraform get with the -upgrade flag only
2.7.2; edit the constraint to allow 3.x and run terraform init again
3.0.0; the pessimistic operator always selects the newest major version
2.7.2; no change is needed because init -upgrade also crosses major versions
quiz.explain: The constraint ~> 2.4 allows 2.4 up to below 3.0, so the newest match, 2.7.2, is installed. Moving to a new major version needs a changed version constraint, and a changed constraint needs a new terraform init to fetch the code.

days.recap: Module sources: ./ local, <NS>/<NAME>/<PROVIDER> registry, git::, s3::, gcs::. Only registries take version. init installs modules into .terraform. Scope is explicit: inputs in via module block, outputs out via module.<label>.<name>. Count and for_each work on modules; keep composition flat.

days.title: State Backends: Local, Locking, Remote State and Backend Configuration

concepts.heading: The Local Backend and Why Teams Outgrow It
concepts.body: With no backend block, Terraform uses the local backend: state is written to terraform.tfstate in the working directory, and the previous version is kept in terraform.tfstate.backup. That is fine for one person learning, and it can be moved with `backend "local" { path = "state/dev.tfstate" }`. The local backend takes a file lock on the machine it runs on, runs operations on that machine, and stores state as plaintext JSON. It cannot share state safely. A common mistake is committing terraform.tfstate to Git so teammates can see it. HashiCorp's guidance is that version control is not a state store: it has no locking, so two applies can overwrite each other, and it gives no way to restrict who can read the secrets that state may hold. The options -state, -state-out and -backup apply to the local backend only, so with an s3 backend they are not a way to read a different state file. The move from local to shared storage is what a remote backend is for.

concepts.heading: Remote Backends and the backend Block
concepts.body: A backend is configured inside the terraform block, and a configuration may contain only one backend block. Only built-in backend types are allowed; you cannot load your own. Remote backends such as s3 keep state off laptops, give everyone the same current copy, and usually add encryption and access control. A typical block is `backend "s3" { bucket = "acme-tf-state" key = "app/prod.tfstate" region = "us-east-1" }`. Backend blocks are read before anything else, so they cannot refer to variables, locals, data sources or other named values: `bucket = var.state_bucket` makes init fail. Credentials should come from environment variables or credential files, not from the block, because the block is written into the .terraform directory and into saved plans. When you add, remove or change a backend, run `terraform init`. Terraform asks whether to copy existing state to the new backend; `-migrate-state` does this explicitly, and `-reconfigure` ignores the old configuration without copying state.

concepts.heading: State Locking
concepts.body: When an operation could write state, the backend locks it so a second run fails fast instead of corrupting the file. Locking is automatic, but only for backends that support it, so check the backend page before assuming it. A second engineer running apply at the same time sees `Error acquiring the state lock` with a lock ID and details about who holds it. Two options tune the behavior: `-lock-timeout=60s` makes Terraform keep retrying for a while before giving up, which suits CI jobs that start just after another ends, and `-lock=false` turns locking off, which removes the protection and is rarely right. If a run was killed and left a stale lock, first confirm nobody is running anything, then release it with `terraform force-unlock LOCK_ID`. Force-unlocking to hurry a colleague's slow apply is dangerous, because two writers then run at once. The command only clears the lock; it does not touch resources or state contents.

concepts.heading: Locking and Settings in the S3 Backend
concepts.body: For the s3 backend the supported lock mechanism is a lock file stored next to the state object in the same bucket, turned on with `use_lockfile = true`. The older method using a DynamoDB table (`dynamodb_table`) is deprecated, so for Terraform 1.12 answers choose use_lockfile and no extra database. It is also wise to enable versioning on the bucket so earlier state versions can be recovered, and `encrypt = true` to encrypt the state object. Per-environment values are supplied with partial configuration: leave the argument out of the block and pass it at init, as in `terraform init -backend-config="bucket=prod-state"` or `-backend-config="prod.s3.tfbackend"`, where the file holds plain `key = "value"` lines. The option can be repeated: command-line options override the same setting in the backend block, and later options override earlier ones. Because a saved plan captures backend settings, do not pass temporary credentials through -backend-config if the plan will be applied later; use environment variables instead.

concepts.heading: The cloud Block and terraform_remote_state
concepts.body: To store state in HCP Terraform you do not write a backend block; you write a cloud block inside the terraform block: `cloud { organization = "acme" workspaces { name = "app-prod" } }`. After `terraform login` and `terraform init`, state lives in that workspace, which also locks and versions it. The same block works for Terraform Enterprise with a hostname argument. Another way teams share information is `data "terraform_remote_state" "net" { backend = "s3" config = {...} }`, which reads another configuration's state. It exposes only the root module outputs of that state, so the producer must declare `output "subnet_id"`, and the reader reaches it as `data.terraform_remote_state.net.outputs.subnet_id`. Reading requires access to the whole state object, including any secrets in it, which is why many teams prefer to publish a few values elsewhere. For example, a network team applies, and the app team reads the subnet ID without copying it by hand.

examPoints: With no backend block Terraform uses the local backend and writes terraform.tfstate plus a .backup copy in the working directory.

Backend blocks cannot use variables or other references; supply per-environment values with `terraform init -backend-config`, where command-line options override the block and later options override earlier ones.
In the s3 backend, `use_lockfile = true` enables locking and DynamoDB locking is deprecated; clear a stale lock only with `terraform force-unlock LOCK_ID` after confirming no run is active.

quiz.q: A pipeline job for the production stack often starts a few seconds before the previous job's apply has released the lock on the s3 backend, and it then fails instantly. The team wants the job to wait and retry without removing the protection. Which change fits?
choices: Add `-lock=false` to the apply command so that the job no longer needs to hold any lock
Run `terraform force-unlock` at the start of every job so that the lock is always free
Add `-lock-timeout=120s` to the plan and apply commands so Terraform retries acquiring the lock
Set `use_lockfile = false` in the backend block so that the lock file is never created
quiz.explain: -lock-timeout keeps retrying a held lock for the given time, then fails, so the lock stays in force. -lock=false and force-unlock both remove the guarantee that only one writer runs at a time, and disabling use_lockfile only removes locking altogether.

quiz.q: A platform team wants the same configuration to use state buckets named `dev-state` and `prod-state` per environment, and they cannot edit the file for each pipeline. Which approach works?
choices: Write `bucket = var.env_bucket` in the backend block and pass `-var` to terraform apply
Leave `bucket` out of the s3 backend block and run `terraform init -backend-config="bucket=prod-state"`
Declare a `locals` value for the bucket name and reference it from the backend block
Use a `data` block to look up the bucket and refer to it inside the backend block
quiz.explain: Partial configuration supplies backend values at init time. Variables, locals and data sources are not available when the backend is read, so the other choices fail during terraform init.

days.recap: Local backend: one machine, plaintext file. Remote backends share state, with locking where supported. Backend blocks take no references; pass values with -backend-config. S3 locks with use_lockfile; force-unlock only stale locks. HCP Terraform uses a cloud block.

days.title: Drift, Refactoring State and Protecting State

concepts.heading: What Drift Is and How a Plan Finds It
concepts.body: Drift is a difference between your real infrastructure and what Terraform's state records, usually because someone changed an object in the console or another tool. Terraform finds it by refreshing: every normal `terraform plan` first reads the current values of the objects in state, then compares them with configuration. If someone changed `instance_type` to a larger size in the console while the configuration says `t3.micro`, plan notes that the object changed outside Terraform and proposes an update in place to bring it back to configuration. Nothing is changed until you apply. If the console change was desired, edit the configuration to match it instead, and the plan becomes empty. If an object was deleted in the console, plan proposes to create it again. This is why a plan is also the cheapest drift check you can run, and why a plan you did not expect to contain changes deserves a look before anyone approves it.

concepts.heading: Refresh-Only Instead of terraform refresh
concepts.body: Sometimes you only want state to record what exists now, without changing any real object. The command for that is `terraform apply -refresh-only`, or `terraform plan -refresh-only` to just preview. Terraform shows the differences it found between state and reality, and when you approve, it writes the new values into state and the outputs; it never creates, updates or destroys infrastructure. The standalone `terraform refresh` command does the same update but without showing you anything first, so the documentation calls it deprecated and recommends -refresh-only, where you can review and cancel. A typical case is a teammate who deleted an instance by hand and wants state to forget it; after approving the refresh-only apply, the resource disappears from state, and the next normal plan will propose to create it again if its block is still in configuration. So refresh-only accepts reality into state, while a normal apply pushes configuration to reality.

concepts.heading: The moved Block for Renames and Refactors
concepts.body: If you rename a resource block from `aws_instance.a` to `aws_instance.b`, Terraform sees a missing resource and a new one, and plans to destroy and create. Tell it they are the same object with a moved block: `moved { from = aws_instance.a to = aws_instance.b }`. The plan then shows the object moving in state, with no replacement. The block also handles moving a resource into a module, renaming a module, or switching between count and for_each, where you need one moved block per instance, for example from `aws_instance.c[0]` to `aws_instance.c["small"]`. Because the block lives in code, a reviewer sees it in the pull request, and every user of a shared module gets the same refactor on their next apply, which is the advantage over `terraform state mv`, a one-off command that edits one state only. Keep historical moved blocks in a published module, since removing them can break users who upgrade from an older version.

concepts.heading: The removed Block and the -replace Option
concepts.body: To stop managing an object without deleting it, use a removed block: `removed { from = aws_s3_bucket.logs lifecycle { destroy = false } }`, and delete the matching resource block. Terraform drops the object from state on apply and the bucket keeps running. The lifecycle block is required in a removed block, and destroy defaults to true: without destroy = false, Terraform removes the object from state and destroys the real object, so that setting is the important line. To rebuild one object that is unhealthy though configuration has not changed, use `terraform apply -replace="aws_instance.web[1]"`. The plan shows the replacement for review, and the option can be repeated for several addresses and applies to that run only. It replaces the older `terraform taint` command, which is deprecated. A related case is an object whose create step failed, for example a provisioner error: Terraform marks it tainted in state, and the next plan proposes to replace it even though no configuration changed. Looking for a `-/+` entry in a plan with an unchanged configuration points to a tainted object.

concepts.heading: Protecting State and Saved Plans
concepts.body: State often holds secrets: database passwords, keys and other attribute values appear in it in plain form, even when marked sensitive, because sensitive only hides them in CLI output. Treat state as a secret store. HashiCorp recommends keeping it in a remote backend, encrypting it at rest and in transit, restricting access with permissions, and keeping audit logs of who reads it. HCP Terraform and the s3 backend with encryption and a restrictive bucket policy are examples. Saved plan files, created with `terraform plan -out=tfplan`, need the same care: they can include sensitive attribute values and the backend settings used when they were created. Uploading a plan as a build artifact that everyone can download is a leak, and so is publishing the output of `terraform show -json`. Never commit state or plan files to version control, and add `*.tfstate` and `*.tfstate.*` to .gitignore as a safety net.

examPoints: A normal plan detects drift through its refresh and proposes to revert it; `terraform apply -refresh-only` updates only state, after review, and replaces the deprecated `terraform refresh`.

Use a moved block to rename or relocate a resource without replacement, one block per instance when changing between count and for_each, and `removed` with `lifecycle { destroy = false }` to forget an object without destroying it.
Replace one unhealthy object with `terraform apply -replace=ADDRESS` (not taint), and protect state and saved plans with remote storage, encryption, access control and audit logs.

quiz.q: An engineer renames `resource "aws_db_instance" "main"` to `"primary"` in a module used by twelve teams. The plan must keep the existing database and also work the same way for every team on its next apply. What should the engineer add to the module?
choices: A `removed` block for aws_db_instance.main with destroy = false, then a new resource block
A note in the README asking each team to run `terraform state mv` before applying
A `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` setting on the renamed resource block
A `moved` block with from = aws_db_instance.main and to = aws_db_instance.primary
quiz.explain: A moved block is stored in code and is applied to each user's state at their next apply, so the database is kept. The removed block would make Terraform forget the object and the new block would then create a second database. state mv works only once per state, and prevent_destroy would make the plan fail rather than avoid the replacement.

quiz.q: A scheduled pipeline runs `terraform plan` nightly and, after someone resized a VM in the console, it shows an in-place update for that VM. The change in the console should stay, and the configuration still lists the old size. What is the best way to end the nightly difference?
choices: Change the configuration to the new size so the plan matches the VM
Run `terraform apply -replace` on the VM so the new size is recorded in configuration
Run `terraform refresh` weekly so the plan no longer notices changes made in the console
Add the VM to `ignore_changes` in the lifecycle block of every other resource in the stack
quiz.explain: Plan compares configuration with real infrastructure, so if the console change is wanted, the configuration must say so; no command rewrites configuration files. A refresh-only apply would update state, but the next plan would still propose reverting the size. The other choices rebuild the VM, use a deprecated command, or apply ignore_changes to the wrong resources.

days.recap: Drift is reality differing from state; plan finds it and proposes a revert. Use apply -refresh-only to accept reality into state after review. moved renames without replacement; removed with lifecycle destroy = false forgets (default is destroy) an object; -replace rebuilds one. State and saved plans are secrets.

days.title: Import, the terraform state Commands and Debug Logging

concepts.heading: Bringing Existing Infrastructure Under Terraform with import
concepts.body: Terraform manages only objects bound to a resource address in state. To adopt something created by hand, add an import block with a matching resource block: `import { to = aws_s3_bucket.logs id = "acme-logs" }`. The `to` argument is the address that will track the object and `id` is the identifier the provider uses, whose exact format is listed on the import section of that resource's provider documentation; guessing it is a common error. The id must be known during planning. Run `terraform plan` and it shows the resource as to be imported; nothing is bound until you apply, so imports are reviewed like any other change, and a missing resource block fails with a message that the configuration for the import target does not exist. An import block with for_each can bring in several objects, addressed with each.key. After an import, run plan again: if it shows an in-place update, your block does not yet match the real object, so adjust the arguments until the plan is empty. Bind each real object to one address only; importing the same ID twice leads to conflicting management.

concepts.heading: The terraform import Command
concepts.body: The older way to adopt an object is the CLI command `terraform import aws_s3_bucket.logs acme-logs`. It needs the resource block to exist first, and it changes state immediately, with no plan to review. It runs locally, so against an HCP Terraform workspace it does not see variables stored in that workspace, and you must supply them another way. Because it writes state at once, the import block is generally preferred: it is declarative, can be reviewed in a pull request, and can be run through CI. The command only touches state and never changes the real object, and importing does not write configuration for you; you must write or adjust the resource block yourself so that plan matches. A short comparison for the exam: import block means plan, review, then apply; terraform import means state edited immediately. Both need the provider to know the ID format of the resource type, and both leave the real object untouched.

concepts.heading: Reading and Editing State with terraform state
concepts.body: The terraform state command group works on state without changing infrastructure. `terraform state list` shows every tracked address; give it an address such as `module.elb` to filter, or `-id=sg-1234abcd` to find which address manages a known real object. `terraform state show aws_instance.web` prints the recorded attributes of one resource and has no side effects. `terraform state pull` prints the raw state JSON, handy for piping into jq. `terraform show` is the related command that renders the latest state, or a saved plan file when you give it one, and `terraform show -json` is machine-readable and exposes sensitive values, so treat its output as secret. Commands that modify state back it up first: `terraform state mv` rebinds an object to a new address, for example `terraform state mv aws_instance.worker aws_instance.helper` after a rename, and `terraform state rm` removes an address from state. Neither changes the real infrastructure.

concepts.heading: state mv and state rm in Practice
concepts.body: Suppose you rename a block from worker to helper. Plan proposes to destroy the old instance and create a new one, because state still holds the old address. Running `terraform state mv aws_instance.worker aws_instance.helper` points the existing object at the new address, and the plan becomes empty. The same command moves a resource into a module: `terraform state mv aws_instance.web module.compute.aws_instance.web`. For shared code, a moved block is the better tool, as it travels with the code. `terraform state rm` makes Terraform forget an object without destroying it, and it is usually paired with deleting the resource block. If you remove only the state entry and leave the block in configuration, the next plan shows the resource as to be created, producing a duplicate. When an address matches many instances, for example `aws_instance.web` created with count, add `-dry-run` to see what it matches before anything is forgotten. Since state-changing subcommands write a backup, a mistake can be undone from that copy.

concepts.heading: Debug Logging with TF_LOG
concepts.body: When an error message is vague, turn on detailed logs with environment variables. `TF_LOG` enables logging and sets the level: TRACE is the most verbose, then DEBUG, INFO, WARN and ERROR. The logs go to stderr, so they mix into the terminal output unless you redirect them. `TF_LOG_PATH=./terraform.log` writes them to a file, but only works when TF_LOG is also set, and the file is appended to on each run, so a persistent CI workspace grows one file. Using a file also keeps the plan text clean for scripts that parse it. `TF_LOG_CORE` and `TF_LOG_PROVIDER` set separate levels for Terraform core and for provider plugins, so you can ask for TRACE from the provider while keeping core at ERROR. Provider logs show the API calls behind errors such as a vague HeadBucket failure. The JSON log format is not stable across versions. When filing a bug report, attach a log; before sharing, look through it for secrets. Unset TF_LOG afterwards to restore normal output.

examPoints: An import block binds one real object (`id`) to one address (`to`) described by a resource block; it is reviewed in plan and takes effect in apply, while `terraform import` edits state immediately.

terraform state list/show/pull read state, while state mv rebinds an object to a new address and state rm forgets it; neither changes real infrastructure, and a block left in configuration after state rm plans to create a new object.
TF_LOG turns logging on (TRACE is most verbose), TF_LOG_PATH only redirects it and appends to the file, and TF_LOG_CORE and TF_LOG_PROVIDER set separate levels.

quiz.q: An engineer has set `TF_LOG_PATH=./debug.log` in a CI job and runs `terraform plan` hoping to capture provider API errors. The job finishes with no debug.log file. What should the engineer add?
choices: Set `TF_LOG_PATH` to an absolute path, because Terraform ignores relative paths for the log file
Set `TF_LOG=DEBUG` or another level, since TF_LOG_PATH only redirects logs that are already enabled
Run `terraform state pull > debug.log` before the plan so that Terraform opens the file
Add `-json` to the plan command so that Terraform writes debug output to a file
quiz.explain: TF_LOG_PATH sets where logs go, while TF_LOG turns them on. Relative paths work, the state pull command prints state rather than logs, and -json changes the plan output format instead of enabling detailed logs.

quiz.q: A teammate ran `terraform state rm aws_sqs_queue.jobs` to stop managing a queue and left the resource block in the configuration. The queue still exists in the cloud account. What does the next `terraform plan` show?
choices: No changes, because the queue still exists and Terraform finds it by name in the account
A destroy for the queue, because the removed state entry marks it as no longer wanted
An error asking for an import block, because a state entry is required for every block
A create for a new queue, because the block has no state entry bound to it
quiz.explain: Terraform decides from state, and with no entry the block looks like a new resource, so plan proposes to create a duplicate. It never searches the account for matching objects, and state rm does not mark anything for destruction.

days.recap: Import blocks adopt one real object into one address and are reviewed in plan. terraform import edits state at once. state list/show/pull read; mv rebinds; rm forgets without touching infrastructure. TF_LOG enables logs, TF_LOG_PATH redirects them.

days.title: HCP Terraform: Workspaces, Workflows, Remote Operations, Variables and the Private Registry

concepts.heading: HCP Terraform Workspaces
concepts.body: HCP Terraform is a hosted service that runs Terraform for teams and stores state, variables, run history and access settings together. The unit it manages is the workspace. An HCP Terraform workspace is a full replacement for a working directory: it holds its own state versions, variables, credentials, run history and team permissions, so each environment or component usually gets one, such as `app-prod` and `app-dev`. This differs from a Terraform CLI workspace, which is only an extra named state file inside one working directory with the same backend and the same variables. Workspaces belong to an organization. You can create one in the UI, with the API, or implicitly, when a cloud block names a workspace that does not exist yet. An implicitly created workspace is remote and empty, so provider credentials must be added as variables before its first run. Locks, state versions and rollbacks are managed per workspace, which is why a single failed run in one workspace does not block the others.

concepts.heading: Three Workflows: CLI, VCS and API
concepts.body: A run in HCP Terraform can start in three ways. In the CLI-driven workflow you keep the configuration locally, add a cloud block, run `terraform login` and then `terraform plan` or `terraform apply`; the work executes in the workspace and the output streams back to your terminal. In the VCS-driven workflow the workspace is linked to a repository and branch: a pull request creates a speculative plan, which is plan-only and can never be applied, and a merge to the tracked branch starts a normal run. In the API-driven workflow your own tooling uploads a configuration version and creates runs over HTTPS, which suits configuration generated by other systems or pipelines with their own triggers. Running `terraform plan` through a cloud block is a remote speculative plan even in a workspace linked to VCS, but a remote `terraform apply` is meant for workspaces without a VCS link. Pick the workflow that matches where the code lives and who decides when to run.

concepts.heading: Remote Operations and Execution Modes
concepts.body: By default a workspace runs plan and apply remotely on HCP Terraform workers. Remote operations stream output to your CLI, use the variables stored in the workspace, run policy checks and are queued per workspace. Runs in one workspace are serialized: while a plan waits for someone to confirm it, later runs queue behind it until it is applied or discarded. Execution mode can be changed. Remote runs on HCP Terraform workers, Agent runs on agents you host, which helps when a target is on a private network, and Local means your own machine does the work while HCP Terraform only stores state. In local mode the workspace variables are ignored and no policy checks or other remote-run features happen, so a team wondering why stored variables are not used after a mode change should check execution mode first. Provider credentials in a workspace are set as environment variables; Terraform variables feed `var.` inputs instead.

concepts.heading: Variables, Sensitive Values and Variable Sets
concepts.body: Workspace variables come in two kinds: Terraform variables, which supply values for `variable` blocks, and environment variables, which set the process environment, for example `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` for a provider. Putting a credential in as a Terraform variable does not reach the provider. A variable marked sensitive is write-only afterwards: the UI and API will not show it again, though it can still reach state or logs if configuration outputs it. A variable set groups variables so they can be applied to many workspaces, or to a whole project, including workspaces created later. For a value defined in several places in a CLI-driven run, command-line values win over workspace variables, which win over variable sets, unless the set is marked as a priority set, which overrides everything. So if a variable set gives instance_type `t3.small`, the workspace gives `t3.large`, and you run `terraform apply -var 'instance_type=t3.micro'`, the command-line value is used.

concepts.heading: The Private Registry and Cross-Workspace State
concepts.body: The private registry lets an organization publish its own versioned modules and providers for its workspaces, in the same style as the public registry. Modules are published from a VCS repository using version tags, and consumers reference them with the `app.terraform.io/acme/vpc/aws` style address and a `version` argument, without needing access to the source repository. The registry shares modules; it does not force their use. To require that every module come from the organization's registry and stop runs that break the rule, you need policy as code, covered on the next day. Workspaces can also exchange data. A downstream workspace can read the root outputs of another with `data "terraform_remote_state"`, but the source workspace must allow it, or you can use the `tfe_outputs` data source from the tfe provider. A run trigger can also start the downstream workspace automatically after the source applies, which is a separate feature taught next. Private registry modules support the same versioning and update workflow as public ones.

examPoints: An HCP Terraform workspace replaces a working directory with state, variables, runs and permissions, whereas a CLI workspace is just an extra state file in one directory.
VCS workflow: pull request means speculative plan, merge means a normal run; CLI workflow: a cloud block with remote runs; API workflow: custom tooling uploads configuration and creates runs.

Provider credentials are environment variables in the workspace, command-line values beat workspace variables which beat non-priority variable sets, and Local execution mode ignores workspace variables and policy checks.

quiz.q: A team connects workspace `shop-stage` to a repository branch. A developer opens a pull request that changes an instance size. What does HCP Terraform do with it before anyone merges?
choices: It starts a speculative plan that shows the proposed changes and cannot be applied
It applies the change to the workspace in a draft state and rolls it back when closed
It queues a normal run that waits for approval and holds back every later run in `shop-stage`
It does nothing until a member of the team manually creates a run in the user interface
quiz.explain: Opening or updating a pull request creates a speculative, plan-only run whose result is posted to the pull request. Only a merge to the tracked branch creates a normal run that can be applied and holds the queue.

quiz.q: A workspace stores `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` as Terraform variables, and the AWS provider reports that no credentials were found. What fixes the problem?
choices: Mark both variables as sensitive so that the provider can read the hidden values at run time
Declare matching `variable` blocks with defaults and refer to them in the provider block
Change both entries to environment variables, which the provider reads from the run's environment
Move both variables into a variable set, since a workspace cannot supply credentials directly
quiz.explain: The provider reads credentials from the process environment, so they must be environment variables. Terraform variables only feed var. inputs, and sensitive or variable sets only change visibility or scope.

days.recap: A workspace is a full working directory with state, variables and permissions. Three workflows: CLI, VCS (pull request = speculative plan) and API. Remote runs use workspace variables; Local mode does not. Credentials are environment variables; variable sets share them. Private registry shares modules.

days.title: HCP Terraform: Projects, Run Triggers, Policy, Teams, Drift Detection and Terraform Enterprise

concepts.heading: Projects and Teams
concepts.body: Projects group workspaces inside an organization so access and settings can be managed in bulk. Suppose 12 networking workspaces and 30 application workspaces exist, and the networking team must manage the first set and see nothing of the second. Put the networking workspaces in a `networking` project and give that team permissions on the project, which is more maintainable than editing 12 workspace permission lists. Teams are groups of users. Permissions can be granted at the organization, project and workspace level, and they add up: a team holding the organization permission to manage all workspaces and only Read on one workspace can still manage that workspace. At workspace level the common roles are Read, Plan, Write and Admin. Plan lets people queue plans and see results but not apply, Write allows applying, and Admin changes settings. Contractors who may propose changes while a staff engineer approves every apply fit Plan for the first group and Write for the second.

concepts.heading: Run Triggers
concepts.body: A run trigger connects workspaces that depend on each other. It is configured on the downstream workspace, which lists a source workspace. When a run in the source applies successfully, HCP Terraform queues a run in the downstream workspace. For example, workspace `app` reads the VPC ID that workspace `network` outputs; adding `network` as the source in a run trigger on `app` means a new plan appears in `app` after each successful apply in `network`. The triggered run is an ordinary run: it is not auto-applied by default and waits for confirmation unless the separate Auto-apply run triggers setting is on in the downstream workspace. It is queued behind any run already waiting in that workspace. A trigger only queues runs; it does not copy values. The downstream configuration still needs a way to read them, such as `terraform_remote_state` or `tfe_outputs`, and the source workspace must permit that access.

concepts.heading: Policy Enforcement with Sentinel and OPA
concepts.body: Policy as code lets an organization check runs against rules. HCP Terraform policies are written in Sentinel or Open Policy Agent (OPA), the two frameworks covered here. Policies are collected into policy sets, and a policy set belongs to one framework and is applied to chosen workspaces or projects, or to every workspace. The checks run against the plan after it is produced and before an apply can start. For Sentinel, an enforcement level decides what a failure does. Advisory only warns and the run continues. Soft mandatory stops the run but an authorized user can override the failure. Hard mandatory stops the run until the problem is fixed, unless the policy set is configured to allow overrides. A rule such as 'every non-root module must come from our private registry' or 'no instance larger than a chosen size' is the kind of check policies do; the registry itself does not enforce it. Policies are not part of the Terraform CLI alone, which is why they appear in questions on HCP Terraform and Terraform Enterprise.

concepts.heading: Health Assessments and Drift Detection
concepts.body: Drift detection in HCP Terraform comes from health assessments, which run on a schedule on a workspace and compare the real infrastructure with your configuration. They report two things: drift, meaning configuration drift from objects changed outside Terraform, and continuous validation, which re-evaluates the custom conditions and check blocks written in configuration. The results appear on the workspace and can trigger notifications. Assessments are report-only: they never modify infrastructure, state or configuration, and a person decides whether to run a plan to revert the drift or update the code. They need the workspace to use Remote or Agent execution, not Local, since HCP Terraform must run the work itself. This differs from a manual `terraform plan` or `terraform apply -refresh-only`, which you start yourself. Together with a scheduled plan in a pipeline, they give an early warning that someone changed a managed object by hand.

concepts.heading: terraform login, the cloud Block and Terraform Enterprise
concepts.body: `terraform login` starts an interactive browser flow that creates an API token and stores it in `credentials.tfrc.json` in the Terraform data directory; automation instead sets a token in a credentials block or the TF_TOKEN_ environment variable. The `cloud` block then selects a workspace by name, or by tags: `workspaces { tags = ["networking"] }`, after which `terraform workspace list`, `select` and `new` operate on the tagged workspaces. Name and tags cannot be combined. When you add a cloud block to a configuration that used the local backend, `terraform init` offers to copy the existing state into the workspace, and you confirm the prompt. Terraform Enterprise is the self-hosted distribution of the same platform, and uses the same cloud block, with a `hostname` set to your instance, such as `tfe.example.com`, and a login to that host. Policy enforcement, the private registry, teams, remote runs and variable sets come from HCP Terraform or Terraform Enterprise, whereas fmt, validate and the dependency lock file are part of the Community CLI.

examPoints: Projects group workspaces so a team can be delegated access to all of them at once; team permissions at organization, project and workspace level add up and the most permissive applies.

A run trigger is set on the downstream workspace, queues a run after a successful source apply, and does not auto-apply by default (separate Auto-apply run triggers setting); policy sets (Sentinel or OPA) check plans before apply, and soft mandatory failures can be overridden.

terraform login stores a token in credentials.tfrc.json, the same cloud block serves HCP Terraform and Terraform Enterprise (with hostname), and health assessments report drift on a schedule without changing anything.

quiz.q: The `billing` team should be able to see and edit settings in all eight workspaces that make up the finance platform, but not in any other workspace of the organization. New finance workspaces will be added over time. What is the most maintainable design?
choices: Create a separate team per workspace and add each billing user to all eight of those teams
Give the billing team the organization permission to manage all workspaces, which includes the finance ones
Share a variable set with the finance workspaces and rely on it to limit who can edit them
Place the finance workspaces in a project and give the billing team access to that project
quiz.explain: A project groups workspaces and a team can be given permissions on the whole project, including workspaces added later. Organization-wide manage permission would reach every workspace, and a variable set shares values and does not control access.

quiz.q: A Sentinel policy set contains a policy at the hard mandatory level that checks every plan for oversized instances. The policy set is not configured to allow overrides. A plan in the workspace `data-prod` fails the policy. What happens to the run?
choices: The run continues to the apply phase, and the failure is only shown as a warning in the run
The run stops until the configuration is changed so the plan passes the policy
The run stops, and an authorized user can override the failure and let the apply proceed
The run is discarded and the workspace is locked until an organization owner unlocks it
quiz.explain: Hard mandatory means the failure blocks the run until the configuration is fixed, since this policy set allows no overrides. Advisory would only warn, and soft mandatory is the level that can be overridden by an authorized user.

days.recap: Projects delegate access to groups of workspaces; team permissions add up. Run triggers (on the downstream workspace) queue a run after a source apply. Sentinel and OPA policy sets check plans before apply. Health assessments report drift only. The same cloud block serves Terraform Enterprise via hostname.

days.title: Final Review: Exam Format, the Eight Objectives, Commonly Confused Pairs and Test-Day Plan

concepts.heading: Know the Exam Format
concepts.body: The HashiCorp Certified: Terraform Associate (004) exam lasts 1 hour, is proctored online, is given in English, costs USD 70.50 and the certification is valid for 2 years. It tests Terraform 1.12 and includes HCP Terraform. Question types are true or false, multiple choice and multiple answer; a multiple answer question says how many to pick, for example 'Pick the 2 correct responses', so read the count and choose exactly that many. The number of questions, the pass mark and the weight of each objective are not published, so do not rely on a rumored number and spread your preparation evenly. The eight objectives are: 1 Infrastructure as Code concepts, 2 Terraform fundamentals (providers and state), 3 core workflow, 4 configuration, 5 modules, 6 state management, 7 maintaining infrastructure with import, state commands and logging, and 8 HCP Terraform. With one hour and an unpublished question count, answer what you know first and flag the rest.

concepts.heading: What Is New in 004
concepts.body: Four topics are new compared with the earlier exam and deserve a final pass. First, depends_on and create_before_destroy appear explicitly in objective 4: depends_on adds a hidden ordering when Terraform cannot see a relationship through references, and create_before_destroy builds the replacement before deleting the old object. Second, custom conditions: preconditions and postconditions inside resources and data sources, and check blocks, which report problems as warnings without stopping a run. Third, ephemeral values and write-only arguments: ephemeral variables and resources are never stored in state or plan, and write-only arguments accept a value without saving it, which keeps secrets out of state; sensitive only hides output. Fourth, in objective 8, workspaces and projects in HCP Terraform, including how they differ from CLI workspaces and how projects delegate access. Also remember the replacements the 004 exam expects: apply -refresh-only instead of terraform refresh, apply -replace instead of taint, and use_lockfile instead of DynamoDB locking in the s3 backend.

concepts.heading: Confused Pairs: Providers, State, Workflow and Configuration
concepts.body: Pairs that look alike are favorite wrong answers. required_providers declares source and version constraints in configuration, while .terraform.lock.hcl records the exact selected versions and checksums; `terraform init -upgrade` updates the lock file within constraints. `init -reconfigure` discards the old backend setup without copying state, while `init -migrate-state` copies state to the new backend. `terraform validate` checks syntax and internal consistency without reading real infrastructure, while `plan` compares with real objects. `plan -out` saves a plan that apply can run without prompting, whereas `-auto-approve` skips the prompt for a fresh plan. `-target` limits a run to chosen addresses for exceptional cases, and `-refresh-only` updates state only. `count` identifies instances by index, so removing a middle item shifts addresses, while `for_each` uses stable keys. A `data` block reads existing objects, a `resource` block manages them. `sensitive` hides values in output only; ephemeral and write-only values stay out of state. `depends_on` orders resources, `lifecycle` changes how they are created, replaced or ignored. A precondition checks inputs before, a postcondition checks results after.

concepts.heading: Confused Pairs: State, Import, Modules and HCP Terraform
concepts.body: Import block versus `terraform import`: the block is reviewed in plan, the command edits state immediately. `moved` renames in code and travels with a shared module, `state mv` is a one-off edit of one state, and `removed` with `lifecycle { destroy = false }` (the default is to destroy) forgets an object, as does `state rm`. `state list` and `state show` read; `state mv` and `state rm` change state and back it up; none touches infrastructure. `-replace` rebuilds one object, `taint` is deprecated. `TF_LOG` turns logs on and `TF_LOG_PATH` only redirects them. `-lock-timeout` waits for a lock, `-lock=false` ignores it, `force-unlock` clears a stale one. A backend block cannot use variables, a cloud block selects an HCP Terraform workspace. A module `source` says where code comes from and `version` works for registry sources only; module outputs are the only values a caller can read. An HCP Terraform workspace is a full working directory; a CLI workspace is just another state file. Projects group workspaces for access; variable sets share variables. Run triggers chain workspaces; policy sets (Sentinel, OPA) check plans; health assessments only report drift.

concepts.heading: Test-Day Plan
concepts.body: Before the exam, sleep, check your identification and set up the proctored environment: a clear desk, a working camera and microphone, a stable connection, and the system check from the exam provider run beforehand. Start the clock with a first pass: answer questions you know at once, mark uncertain ones and keep moving. For each question, read the last line first to see what is asked, then the stem for deciding clues: a command name, a Terraform version, a block type, whether the object already exists, whether state or real infrastructure changes. On multiple answer items, find the count in the question and eliminate options that are deprecated, experimental or too broad. When two options both seem right, ask which one the documentation recommends (-refresh-only, -replace, use_lockfile, import block, moved block). Use remaining time for marked items, and change an answer only when you can name the clue that makes the new one better. Afterwards, whatever happens, keep a list of topics that felt weak; the bank questions for those objectives are the best next practice.

examPoints: The exam is 1 hour, online proctored, in English, tests Terraform 1.12 and includes HCP Terraform; question types are true or false, multiple choice and multiple answer, and the number of questions, pass mark and weights are not published.
The new topics in 004 are depends_on and create_before_destroy, custom conditions, ephemeral values and write-only arguments, and HCP Terraform workspaces and projects.

Questions that pair look-alike features, such as moved and state mv, validate and plan, sensitive and ephemeral, or an HCP Terraform workspace and a CLI workspace, test which one fits the exact need in the stem.

quiz.q: A configuration manages a database password. The team wants the password never to be written to state or plan files, and the output of `terraform plan` should also not display it. Which combination meets this on Terraform 1.12?
choices: Mark the variable sensitive, which keeps the value out of state and plan files as well as output
Store the password in a local value and add the file to .gitignore, so it never reaches state
Pass the value through an ephemeral variable and use it in a write-only argument of the resource
Place the password in a variable set in HCP Terraform, which prevents it from entering state
quiz.explain: Ephemeral values are not stored in state or plan, and a write-only argument accepts a value without saving it. Sensitive only hides the value in CLI output while state still holds it, and ignoring a file or using a variable set does not change what Terraform writes to state.

quiz.q: An instance in a workspace is degraded, the configuration is unchanged, and the team wants one rebuild that appears in the plan for review before anything is touched. What is the current recommended approach?
choices: Run `terraform taint` on the instance, then let any teammate's next plan pick it up
Run `terraform apply -replace=aws_instance.app` and review the proposed replacement
Run `terraform apply -target=aws_instance.app`, which always rebuilds that instance
Run `terraform refresh` so that Terraform notices the degraded instance and rebuilds it
quiz.explain: The -replace option shows the replacement in the plan for review and applies to that run only. taint is deprecated and lets others plan against the tainted object before review, -target only limits the scope of a run without forcing a rebuild, and refresh only updates state.

days.recap: Format: 1 hour, proctored, 1.12, USD 70.50, three question types, weights and count unpublished. New in 004: depends_on, create_before_destroy, custom conditions, ephemeral and write-only values, HCP workspaces and projects. Read counts and the deciding clue; prefer current, documented commands.
